overview.description: Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas — a vital dual-function gland located behind the stomach in the retroperitoneum — responsible for producing digestive enzymes (exocrine function: amylase, lipase, trypsinogen, elastase, phospholipase) and hormones regulating blood glucose (endocrine function: insulin from beta cells, glucagon from alpha cells, somatostatin from delta cells). Pancreatitis occurs when the pancreas's own digestive enzymes are prematurely activated within the gland itself — rather than in the duodenum where they normally activate — causing autodigestion of the pancreatic tissue, inflammation, oedema, and in severe cases haemorrhage and necrosis. The disease presents across a clinical spectrum from mild self-limiting acute pancreatitis (resolving within days with simple supportive care) to devastating severe necrotising pancreatitis with multi-organ failure and mortality exceeding 30-40%. Chronic pancreatitis represents irreversible progressive fibrosis and destruction of both exocrine and endocrine pancreatic tissue, leading to fat malabsorption, steatorrhoea, malnutrition, and a unique form of diabetes (Type 3c pancreatogenic diabetes). Globally, the two dominant causes of pancreatitis are gallstones (40-50% of acute episodes) and alcohol (25-35%); however, India presents a uniquely important variant — Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis (TCP) — a form of chronic pancreatitis affecting young non-alcoholic individuals predominantly in Southern India (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka) and associated with protein-calorie malnutrition, cassava consumption, and genetic susceptibility. TCP (also termed Fibrocalculous Pancreatic Diabetes — FCPD when diabetes develops) is a South Asian-specific disease largely unknown in the Western world, and it represents one of the most important and distinctive forms of pancreatitis in the Indian context. Management of pancreatitis requires a multidisciplinary team — gastroenterologist, interventional radiologist, pancreatic surgeon, endocrinologist, and dietitian — reflecting the complexity and systemic impact of this condition.
overview.affected_organ: Pancreas (exocrine acinar cells, ductal epithelium, islets of Langerhans); secondary involvement: retroperitoneal fat (peripancreatic necrosis), peritoneum, pleura, lungs (ARDS), kidneys, cardiovascular system, liver, biliary tree
overview.prevalence: Acute pancreatitis: 13-45 cases per 100,000 population annually; approximately 300,000 hospital admissions per year in India; 80% mild; 20% severe; overall mortality 2-3% (mild) rising to 30-40% in severe necrotising pancreatitis; Chronic pancreatitis: 5-12 per 100,000 in Western countries; India: estimated 125 per 100,000 in Southern India (unusually high due to Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis); Kerala has the world's highest prevalence of Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis — approximately 100-200 cases per 100,000 population in some districts
overview.age_group: Acute pancreatitis: all ages; gallstone pancreatitis peaks in women aged 40-60 years; alcoholic pancreatitis in men aged 30-50 years; Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis: uniquely affects young adults aged 10-30 years (onset in adolescence or early adulthood); Autoimmune pancreatitis Type 1: predominantly men over 50 years; Hereditary pancreatitis: childhood onset
overview.is_curable_note: Acute pancreatitis is fully reversible with appropriate treatment in most cases; chronic pancreatitis causes IRREVERSIBLE structural damage — treatment manages symptoms, prevents progression, and addresses complications but cannot restore normal pancreatic architecture; autoimmune pancreatitis Type 1 is uniquely steroid-responsive and may achieve complete remission
overview.is_chronic_note: Acute pancreatitis is episodic and reversible; chronic pancreatitis is irreversible and progressive; recurrent acute pancreatitis leads to chronic pancreatitis in 30-40% of cases
overview.key_fact: Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis (TCP) is a disease unique to South and Southeast Asia — India accounts for more cases than any other country. Unlike Western chronic pancreatitis (which predominantly affects middle-aged alcoholic men), TCP strikes young people aged 10-30 years from low-income backgrounds in southern India, causing severe pancreatic destruction, diabetes in adolescence, and early pancreatic cancer risk. Early diagnosis, nutritional rehabilitation, alcohol and tobacco cessation, and genetic counselling are critical for this distinctive Indian disease.

types.name: Acute Pancreatitis — Revised Atlanta Classification
types.description: An acute inflammatory process of the pancreas with variable involvement of regional tissues or remote organ systems. The Revised Atlanta Classification (2012) is the internationally accepted framework for defining severity, local complications, and clinical phases of acute pancreatitis.

severity_grades.criteria: No organ failure; no local or systemic complications; pancreatic and peripancreatic tissue intact
severity_grades.clinical_course: Self-limiting; resolves within 3-5 days; responds to supportive care (IV fluids, analgesia, early oral refeeding); very low mortality (<1%); no ICU required; may be managed in general medical ward
severity_grades.management: IV Ringer's Lactate (aggressive early resuscitation); adequate analgesia; antiemetics; early oral refeeding (within 24-48 hours as tolerated); no routine antibiotics; no prophylactic antibiotics; discharge when tolerating oral diet and pain controlled

severity_grades.criteria: Transient organ failure (resolves within 48 hours); OR local complications (acute peripancreatic fluid collections, acute necrotic collections) WITHOUT persistent organ failure
severity_grades.clinical_course: Prolonged hospital admission (typically 1-3 weeks); CT scan required to assess local complications; may require intensive monitoring; mortality approximately 5-10%
severity_grades.management: IV fluid resuscitation; analgesia; HDU/ICU monitoring; CT scan at 48-72 hours (or earlier if deteriorating); enteral nutrition (nasogastric or nasojejunal tube feed if not tolerating oral); interventional radiology involvement if collections develop

severity_grades.criteria: Persistent organ failure (>48 hours) in one or more organs: respiratory (PaO2/FiO2 <300 or SpO2 <90% on air), renal (creatinine >170 mcmol/L), cardiovascular (systolic BP <90 mmHg despite fluid resuscitation)
severity_grades.clinical_course: ICU admission mandatory; prolonged hospitalisation (weeks to months); high risk of infected necrosis; multiple organ failure; multiple operative interventions may be needed; mortality 30-40% (higher with infected necrosis without adequate drainage)
severity_grades.management: ICU; aggressive IV resuscitation; mechanical ventilation if ARDS; vasopressors for cardiovascular failure; renal replacement therapy (dialysis) for severe AKI; enteral nutrition via NJT; antibiotics ONLY if infected necrosis confirmed (not prophylactic); minimally invasive step-up approach for necrotic collections (radiological drainage → endoscopic → surgical)

clinical_phases.early_phase_week_1_to_2: Dominated by SIRS (Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome) and early organ failure; the patient is critically ill from systemic cytokine release; necrotising pancreatitis not yet delineated; CT scan not diagnostic of necrosis until 48-72 hours after onset (pancreatic necrosis takes time to demarcate)
clinical_phases.late_phase_after_week_2: Dominated by LOCAL COMPLICATIONS — necrotic collections; infected necrosis (secondary bacterial infection of devitalised pancreatic tissue); walled-off necrosis (WON — the mature form of organised necrotic collection after 4+ weeks)

local_complications.name: Acute Peripancreatic Fluid Collection (APFC)
local_complications.description: Homogeneous fluid collection adjacent to the pancreas, within the first 4 weeks, without a defined wall, in the setting of oedematous (interstitial) pancreatitis; majority resolve spontaneously without intervention

local_complications.name: Pancreatic Pseudocyst
local_complications.description: A well-defined fluid collection with a non-epithelised fibrous wall encapsulating pancreatic juice — forms from APFC after 4+ weeks; contains no solid material (distinguishing from walled-off necrosis); usually results from pancreatic ductal disruption; 40-50% resolve spontaneously; requires intervention if symptomatic (pain, obstruction, infection), enlarging, or causing complications

local_complications.name: Acute Necrotic Collection (ANC)
local_complications.description: A collection containing variable amounts of fluid AND necrotic pancreatic or peripancreatic tissue — occurs within the first 4 weeks in the context of necrotising pancreatitis; may be sterile or infected; distinguished from APFC by heterogeneous content and the presence of necrosis

local_complications.name: Walled-Off Necrosis (WON)
local_complications.description: The mature encapsulated form of ANC — forms after 4+ weeks with development of a well-defined wall; contains heterogeneous solid necrotic material and fluid; the most complex local complication requiring endoscopic or surgical debridement if infected or symptomatic; distinguished from pseudocyst by solid necrotic debris within the collection (visible on CT/MRI)

local_complications.name: Infected Necrosis
local_complications.description: Secondary bacterial infection of pancreatic and/or peripancreatic necrotic tissue — the most life-threatening local complication; occurs in 30-40% of necrotising pancreatitis; indicated by gas within the necrotic collection on CT (pathognomonic); confirmed by CT-guided fine needle aspiration (FNA) for Gram stain and culture; organisms: E. coli, Klebsiella, Enterococcus, Staphylococcus, Bacteroides, Candida (particularly in patients on broad-spectrum antibiotics); management: STEP-UP APPROACH (minimally invasive drainage before surgery); meropenem IV; endoscopic transluminal drainage (through gastric wall); video-assisted retroperitoneal debridement (VARD); surgical necrosectomy as last resort

scoring_systems.score: BISAP Score (Bedside Index for Severity in Acute Pancreatitis)
scoring_systems.variables: BUN >25 mg/dL (1 point); Impaired mental status (1 point); SIRS — 2+ of: temp >38°C or <36°C; HR >90; RR >20; WBC >12,000 or <4,000 (1 point); Age >60 years (1 point); Pleural effusion on imaging (1 point); Maximum 5 points
scoring_systems.interpretation: Score 0-2: low mortality (<2%); Score 3: 5-10% mortality; Score 4-5: 15-20% mortality
scoring_systems.use: Simple bedside scoring at admission; no specialist equipment required; validated in multiple populations including India

scoring_systems.score: CT Severity Index (CTSI / Modified Balthazar Score)
scoring_systems.variables: Balthazar CT grade (A-E: 0-4 points based on degree of pancreatic/peripancreatic inflammation) + Necrosis score (0 = no necrosis; 2 = <30%; 4 = 30-50%; 6 = >50%); Maximum 10 points
scoring_systems.interpretation: Score 0-3: low severity (0-3% mortality); Score 4-6: intermediate (8% morbidity, 3% mortality); Score 7-10: severe (17% morbidity, 17% mortality)
scoring_systems.use: Performed on contrast-enhanced CT at 48-72 hours after onset; defines necrosis extent; guides management; predicts need for intervention

scoring_systems.score: Revised Atlanta Classification Organ Failure Assessment
scoring_systems.variables: Modified Marshall Scoring System: respiratory (PaO2/FiO2 ratio); renal (creatinine); cardiovascular (systolic BP); score ≥2 in any system = organ failure; persistent if >48 hours
scoring_systems.use: Defines severity grade; guides ICU admission; monitors clinical progress

types.name: Necrotising Pancreatitis
types.description: A subtype of severe acute pancreatitis characterised by necrosis (death) of pancreatic parenchyma and/or peripancreatic fat — occurring in approximately 20-30% of severe acute pancreatitis cases and carrying significantly higher morbidity and mortality. Pancreatic necrosis results from ischaemia of the pancreatic microcirculation from severe inflammatory vasospasm, proteolytic enzyme digestion of blood vessel walls, and pancreatic compartment syndrome. The extent of necrosis (partial vs total, sterile vs infected) determines severity and management strategy.
types.pathogenesis: Severe SIRS → release of inflammatory cytokines (TNF-alpha, IL-1, IL-6, IL-8, platelet-activating factor) → vasoconstriction of pancreatic microcirculation → ischaemia → coagulation necrosis of acinar cells; secondary bacterial infection from: bacterial translocation from colon (disrupted gut barrier); haematogenous seeding; biliary organisms
types.diagnosis: CONTRAST-ENHANCED CT SCAN (CECT): areas of non-enhancement after IV contrast in the pancreatic parenchyma = necrosis; cannot be performed until at least 48-72 hours after onset (early CECT overestimates or underestimates necrosis extent); MRI/MRCP superior to CT for characterising WON content (solid vs liquid); endoscopic ultrasound (EUS) guides drainage procedures
types.management_step_up_approach: The 'Step-Up Approach' — progressing from less to more invasive interventions — is the internationally endorsed standard of care for infected necrotising pancreatitis: Step 1: IV antibiotics (meropenem or imipenem — penetrate pancreatic necrosis); Step 2: CT-guided percutaneous catheter drainage (PCD); Step 3: Endoscopic transluminal drainage (EUS-guided through gastric/duodenal wall — endoscopic necrosectomy); Step 4: Video-Assisted Retroperitoneal Debridement (VARD) or laparoscopic necrosectomy; Step 5: Open surgical necrosectomy (last resort — highest morbidity and mortality; reserved for failure of all minimally invasive approaches); The Dutch PANTER trial established that step-up approach has lower mortality and complications than primary open necrosectomy
types.antibiotic_use: Antibiotics ONLY for CONFIRMED INFECTED NECROSIS (not prophylactic): meropenem 1-2g IV every 8 hours OR imipenem-cilastatin 500 mg IV every 6 hours (both achieve excellent pancreatic tissue penetration — unlike many antibiotics that do not penetrate the blood-pancreatic barrier); duration: 14-21 days; add fluconazole if Candida identified in cultures; send CT-FNA culture before starting if possible (though empirical antibiotics appropriate if severe sepsis)

types.name: Chronic Pancreatitis
types.description: A syndrome characterised by irreversible, progressive fibro-inflammatory destruction of both exocrine and endocrine pancreatic tissue — resulting in permanent impairment of digestive enzyme production (exocrine pancreatic insufficiency — EPI) and loss of insulin-secreting beta cells (Type 3c pancreatogenic diabetes). Unlike acute pancreatitis which is episodic and potentially fully reversible, chronic pancreatitis causes permanent structural changes (fibrosis, ductal strictures, intraductal calcifications/stones) that cannot be restored to normal.
types.global_causes: Alcohol (most common globally — 60-70% in Western countries; 40-50% in India); idiopathic; tropical (South/Southeast Asia); hereditary/genetic; autoimmune; obstructive (ductal stricture, pancreas divisum, trauma); hypercalcaemia; hyperlipidaemia; TIGAR-O classification: Toxic/Metabolic; Idiopathic; Genetic; Autoimmune; Recurrent acute pancreatitis; Obstructive

subtypes.description: The most common form in Western countries and a major form in India. Requires sustained heavy alcohol use (typically >5-10 years of drinking >80 g ethanol/day). Alcohol directly damages acinar cells, promotes ductal protein plug formation, and increases ductal pressure. SMOKING is a critical co-factor — acts synergistically with alcohol to accelerate pancreatic fibrosis and is an independent risk factor for chronic pancreatitis even without alcohol.
subtypes.clinical_features: Recurrent episodes of acute-on-chronic pancreatitis; chronic abdominal pain (cardinal symptom — upper abdominal, radiating to back; constant or episodic; often severe and debilitating); weight loss; steatorrhoea (later stages when >90% exocrine function lost); pancreatic calcifications on imaging; dilated main pancreatic duct with ductal stones
subtypes.management: ALCOHOL AND TOBACCO CESSATION (most critical interventions — the only interventions shown to slow progression); pain management; PERT; nutrition

subtypes.subtype: Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis (TCP) / Fibrocalculous Pancreatic Diabetes (FCPD) — INDIA-SPECIFIC
subtypes.description: A form of chronic pancreatitis unique to South and Southeast Asia — predominantly India (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh), with lower prevalence in Bangladesh, Nigeria, and Brazil. India has the world's highest absolute number of TCP cases — with Kerala having particularly high concentration. TCP affects young non-alcoholic individuals (typically ages 10-30 years) from rural low-income backgrounds, causing severe pancreatic destruction with massive intraductal calculi, extreme ductal dilation, and rapid progression to endocrine (FCPD — pancreatogenic diabetes) and exocrine insufficiency.
subtypes.epidemiology: Estimated 125 per 100,000 population in South India; Kerala has world's highest density; predominantly young rural individuals from low-income agricultural backgrounds; male:female ratio approximately 2:1; non-alcoholic by definition
subtypes.aetiology: Multifactorial — not fully elucidated; factors implicated: PROTEIN-CALORIE MALNUTRITION (undernutrition in childhood reduces pancreatic secretory inhibitors — particularly PSTI/SPINK1 — allowing trypsinogen self-activation); CASSAVA CONSUMPTION — cyanogenic glycosides (linamarin) in inadequately processed cassava root → hydrogen cyanide → cytotoxic to pancreatic acinar cells (the cassava hypothesis); GENETIC susceptibility: SPINK1 (N34S) mutations in serine protease inhibitor Kazal type 1 — found in 25-40% of TCP patients vs 2% general population; CLDN2, CTRC, and other trypsinogen pathway gene variants; OXIDATIVE STRESS from micronutrient deficiencies (selenium, zinc, Vitamin C and E); Possibly MICROBIOME dysbiosis from nutritional poverty
clinical_features: YOUNG AGE of presentation — typically 10-30 years (much younger than alcoholic chronic pancreatitis)
PAINFUL TCP (majority): severe intermittent upper abdominal pain radiating to back; in adolescents; nutritional failure
PAINLESS TCP (minority): presents directly with diabetes and steatorrhoea without significant pain history
MASSIVE INTRADUCTAL CALCULI — large, dense stones within the main pancreatic duct (pathognomonic); visible on plain abdominal X-ray as 'chain-like' calcifications across the epigastrium
EXTREME PANCREATIC DUCTAL DILATION — duct diameters 5-15 mm (normal <3 mm); 'chain-of-lakes' appearance on MRCP
MALNUTRITION AND GROWTH FAILURE — stunting; poor nutritional status; low BMI

FIBROCALCULOUS PANCREATIC DIABETES (FCPD) — Type 3c diabetes developing in 30-60% of TCP patients; typically requires insulin; characterized by relative ketoacidosis resistance; hypoglycaemia unawareness; prone to hypoglycaemia; no significant C-peptide despite requiring insulin; associated with higher HbA1c and diabetic complications
subtypes.imaging: Plain X-ray abdomen: PANCREATIC CALCIFICATIONS (pathognomonic — dense speckled or 'chain-of-lakes' calcifications along pancreatic axis in epigastrium); CT: large calculi + dilated duct; MRCP: marked ductal dilation; stones as filling defects
subtypes.management: Nutritional rehabilitation (high-calorie, high-protein, low-fat diet); pancreatic enzyme replacement (PERT) — vital; insulin for FCPD; pain management (ERCP with endoscopic stone extraction, endoscopic pancreatic stenting, extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy — ESWL; lateral pancreaticojejunostomy — Puestow procedure for large duct dilation); antioxidant supplementation (Vitamin C, E, selenium, beta-carotene, methionine); genetic counselling (SPINK1 mutation); cancer surveillance (elevated pancreatic cancer risk)
subtypes.pancreatic_cancer_risk: TCP/FCPD carries significantly elevated pancreatic cancer risk (5-10× general population); EUS and CT surveillance recommended every 1-2 years in established TCP; any new pain change, weight loss, or rising CA 19-9 in a TCP patient warrants urgent investigation
subtypes.india_significance: TCP is a disease of poverty and malnutrition in India; nutritional programmes (mid-day meal schemes, anganwadi supplementation, cassava processing education) are fundamental public health interventions; SPINK1 N34S genetic testing available at AIIMS, PGI Chandigarh, and major medical centres; the Prasad scale and Balakrishnan classification are India-specific TCP staging systems

subtypes.description: A unique steroid-responsive form of chronic pancreatitis — distinguished from other forms by its dramatic response to corticosteroids, distinct histopathological and imaging features, and frequent association with other IgG4-related diseases. Two distinct types:

type_1_AIP.description: IgG4-Related Disease (IgG4-RD) — part of a multisystem fibro-inflammatory disorder affecting pancreas, bile ducts (IgG4-sclerosing cholangitis), kidneys, retroperitoneum, lungs, and salivary glands; predominantly affects men over 50; often presents as obstructive jaundice (mimicking pancreatic cancer — the most important differential diagnosis)
type_1_AIP.imaging: Diffuse sausage-like pancreatic enlargement (classic — 'sausage pancreas'); featureless margin; peripheral rim of reduced enhancement ('halo sign' on CT); capsule-like rim; strictured irregular main pancreatic duct without upstream dilation (differs from pancreatic cancer where obstruction causes upstream dilation)
type_1_AIP.diagnosis: HISORT criteria (Histology, Imaging, Serology, Other organ involvement, Response to steroids); Serum IgG4 elevated (>2× ULN is highly specific — though elevated IgG4 found in 5-10% of pancreatic cancer); tissue biopsy for LPSP (lymphoplasmacytic sclerosing pancreatitis) with IgG4-positive plasma cells >10/HPF
type_1_AIP.treatment: Prednisolone 40 mg/day for 4 weeks then taper over 3-6 months; dramatic complete radiological and clinical response; relapse in 30-40% requiring maintenance steroid or azathioprine
type_1_AIP.critical_differential: AIP vs pancreatic cancer: THE MOST IMPORTANT DIFFERENTIAL in clinical practice; a middle-aged man with obstructive jaundice, pancreatic mass, and elevated CA 19-9 could have either; misdiagnosing AIP as cancer leads to unnecessary Whipple surgery; misdiagnosing cancer as AIP leads to fatal delay in surgery; empirical steroid trial (2 weeks of prednisolone) with strict monitoring is sometimes used when imaging and serology are not conclusive — cancer does not respond to steroids

type_2_AIP.description: Idiopathic duct-centric pancreatitis (IDCP) — granulocytic epithelial lesions (GEL) in pancreatic ducts; NOT associated with IgG4; serum IgG4 normal; associated with inflammatory bowel disease (IBD — Crohn's, UC) in 20-30%; younger age than Type 1; also steroid-responsive
type_2_AIP.treatment: Prednisolone as for Type 1; lower relapse rate than Type 1

subtypes.description: Caused by gain-of-function mutations in trypsinogen genes or loss-of-function mutations in pancreatic protease inhibitor genes — resulting in premature trypsinogen activation and autodigestion from childhood. Rare but important for genetic counselling and cancer surveillance.
genetic_causes: PRSS1 (Cationic trypsinogen) mutations — R122H and N29I are most common; autosomal dominant; high penetrance; most common cause of hereditary pancreatitis
SPINK1 (N34S) — serine protease inhibitor Kazal type 1; loss of trypsin inhibition; associated with TCP in India AND hereditary pancreatitis in West; autosomal recessive with reduced penetrance
CFTR mutations — cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator; heterozygous mutations predispose to chronic pancreatitis; also causes CFRD (cystic fibrosis-related diabetes)
CTRC (Chymotrypsin C) mutations — reduces protective trypsin degradation
subtypes.clinical_features: Onset in childhood or early adolescence; recurrent acute pancreatitis episodes from age <20 years; family history; VERY HIGH PANCREATIC CANCER RISK (50-70× general population — lifetime cumulative risk 25-40%); requires annual EUS surveillance from age 40 years
subtypes.management: Genetic counselling; alcohol and smoking cessation mandatory; pain management; PERT; ERCP; surgery; annual pancreatic cancer surveillance; total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation (TP-IAT) for intractable pain in young patients with hereditary pancreatitis — prevents post-pancreatectomy diabetes

types.name: Groove Pancreatitis
types.description: A rare but distinct form of chronic pancreatitis affecting the 'groove' area between the pancreatic head, duodenum, and common bile duct — causing fibrous scar tissue in this anatomical compartment. Predominantly affects middle-aged men with heavy alcohol use. The groove fibrosis narrows the duodenum (duodenal stenosis) causing vomiting and weight loss, and may obstruct the CBD (causing jaundice). Imaging: scar-like mass with sheet-like fibrosis in the pancreatico-duodenal groove; may be indistinguishable from pancreatic cancer on CT — duodenal wall thickening with cyst-like spaces is more typical of groove pancreatitis than cancer.
types.management: Alcohol cessation; PPI; conservative management; pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure) when cannot exclude cancer or for intractable symptoms

types.name: Drug-Induced Acute Pancreatitis
types.description: Approximately 1.5-2% of acute pancreatitis cases are drug-induced. Requires clinical suspicion, temporal association (onset after drug initiation), exclusion of other causes, and resolution after drug withdrawal.
class_I_drugs_definite_causation: Azathioprine and 6-mercaptopurine (IBD treatment — most common drug cause; dose-dependent)
class_II_drugs_probable: GLP-1 agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide, exenatide — emerging evidence; post-marketing surveillance ongoing)
DPP-4 inhibitors (sitagliptin, vildagliptin — signal in pharmacovigilance data)
types.management: Stop the causative drug; supportive treatment; rechallenge NOT recommended in most cases (risk of recurrence)

severity_levels.name: Mild Acute Pancreatitis or Controlled Chronic Pancreatitis
severity_levels.description: Acute: self-limiting without organ failure or necrosis. Chronic: stable, controlled symptoms with adequate nutritional and glycaemic management.
severity_levels.criteria: Acute: no organ failure (Marshall score <2); no local complications; BISAP ≤2; CRP <150 mg/L at 48h; no necrosis on CT; Chronic: pain controlled; no active acute-on-chronic episode; adequate nutrition (BMI >18.5); PERT dose optimised; HbA1c controlled; no complications
severity_levels.functional_impact: Mild discomfort; able to eat; weight stable; may be managed outpatient
severity_levels.management: Acute: IV Ringer's Lactate; analgesia; antiemetics; oral refeeding within 24-48h; discharge in 3-5 days; cholecystectomy before discharge or within 2 weeks if gallstone aetiology; Chronic: PERT with meals; insulin if FCPD; low-fat diet; alcohol and tobacco cessation; pain management

severity_levels.name: Moderately Severe Acute Pancreatitis or Exacerbated Chronic Pancreatitis
severity_levels.description: Acute: local complications or transient organ failure <48 hours. Chronic: acute-on-chronic episode; uncontrolled pain requiring escalation.
severity_levels.criteria: Acute: BISAP 3; CRP >150 mg/L; local fluid collections; CT showing peripancreatic changes; Chronic: pain uncontrolled on current regimen; active acute-on-chronic episode; malnutrition (weight loss >10%); FCPD with poor glycaemic control
severity_levels.functional_impact: Unable to eat; significant pain; hospital admission required; activity severely limited
severity_levels.management: Hospital admission; IV fluids; IV analgesia; CT scan at 48-72h; enteral nutrition (NG tube feed); HDU monitoring; drain collections if symptomatic; adjust pain medications; GI and nutrition specialist review

severity_levels.name: Severe Acute Pancreatitis with Persistent Organ Failure
severity_levels.description: Persistent single or multi-organ failure >48 hours — the defining feature of severe acute pancreatitis.
severity_levels.criteria: Persistent organ failure (respiratory: SpO2 <90% or PaO2/FiO2 <300; renal: creatinine >170 mcmol/L; cardiovascular: SBP <90 despite fluids); BISAP 4-5; CRP >300 mg/L; CT severity index ≥7; extensive necrosis on CT
severity_levels.functional_impact: ICU dependent; ventilated; dialysis; TPN or NJT feeds; completely incapacitated
severity_levels.management: ICU mandatory; aggressive resuscitation; vasopressors; mechanical ventilation; renal replacement therapy; enteral nutrition via NJT (superior to TPN — maintains gut barrier, reduces bacterial translocation, reduces infectious complications); CT-guided drainage if infected necrosis; step-up surgical approach; multidisciplinary team

severity_levels.name: Critical — Infected Necrosis, Septic Shock, Multi-Organ Failure
severity_levels.description: Life-threatening complications with infected pancreatic necrosis, septic shock, and multiple organ failure — the most lethal presentation of pancreatitis.
severity_levels.criteria: Infected necrosis (gas in necrotic collection on CT; FNA positive culture; worsening despite antibiotics); septic shock (hypotension + lactate >2 mmol/L); multi-organ failure (≥2 organ systems); APACHE II score >20
severity_levels.management: EMERGENCY: ICU; IV meropenem or imipenem; source control by step-up approach (EUS-guided drainage → VARD → open necrosectomy); vasopressors; ventilation; dialysis; nutritional support; surgical team involvement; mortality 30-40%

causes.mnemonic: I GET SMASHED — a comprehensive aetiological mnemonic for acute pancreatitis

causes_detailed.details: No identifiable cause after standard evaluation; many 'idiopathic' cases are actually due to: biliary microlithiasis (tiny stones <2 mm not visible on ultrasound — identified on EUS or biliary drainage microscopy with polarised light); sphincter of Oddi dysfunction (SOD); occult genetic mutation; small ampullary tumours; a thorough search including EUS, genetic testing, and MRCP reduces idiopathic proportion to <5%

causes_detailed.proportion: 40-50% of acute pancreatitis — the most common cause
causes_detailed.details: Small stones (<5 mm) more likely to cause pancreatitis (pass through cystic duct more easily and impact at the ampulla); impacted stone at ampulla of Vater → biliary and pancreatic obstruction simultaneously → intraductal hypertension → trypsinogen activation; CHOLECYSTECTOMY should be performed during the same admission (mild pancreatitis) or within 2 weeks (moderately severe) to prevent recurrence — recurrence rate without cholecystectomy: 25-30% within 6 weeks; ERCP within 24-72 hours if concurrent cholangitis or persistent CBD obstruction

causes_detailed.proportion: 25-35% globally; 40-50% in India for acute pancreatitis; 60-70% for chronic pancreatitis
causes_detailed.details: Ethanol increases pancreatic secretion while simultaneously causing ductal protein plug formation; acetaldehyde (ethanol metabolite) is directly cytotoxic to acinar cells; alcohol sensitises the pancreas to other triggers; typically requires years of heavy drinking (>5-10 years) before chronic pancreatitis develops; acute alcoholic pancreatitis may occur at any point in this timeline; alcohol + smoking acts synergistically — together accelerate chronic pancreatitis by 5-fold

causes_detailed.proportion: Trauma: 1-2%; Post-ERCP pancreatitis: 3-5% of all ERCPs (the most common serious complication of ERCP)
causes_detailed.details: Blunt abdominal trauma (steering wheel, handlebars — epigastric compression); post-ERCP pancreatitis: prevented by rectal indomethacin 100 mg suppository immediately post-procedure (reduces PEP by 50-60%), aggressive IV fluid resuscitation; pancreatic stent placement in high-risk ERCP; post-ERCP pancreatitis can be very severe despite relatively low doses of contrast
See Type 05 (Drug-induced pancreatitis) above for full drug list

Mumps virus (paramyxovirus) — tropism for pancreatic acinar cells and salivary glands; pancreatitis in mumps is usually mild; other viruses: Coxsackie B; CMV (in immunocompromised); HIV (direct acinar injury + antiretrovirals); Hepatitis B; EBV; COVID-19 (acute COVID and MIS-C in children)

Tityus trinitatis (Trinidad); MESOBUTHUS TAMULUS (INDIAN RED SCORPION — Mesobuthus tamulus; also called Buthus tamulus) — the most medically important scorpion in India; predominantly in Maharashtra, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat; causes systemic envenomation including ACUTE PANCREATITIS (mechanism: massive sympathetic and parasympathetic nerve stimulation → cholecystokinin-like hyperstimulation of pancreatic acinar cells → premature enzyme activation → acute pancreatitis); also causes cardiovascular toxicity, pulmonary oedema, myocarditis; management: prazosin (alpha-blocker — reverses sympathetic overactivation; reduces pancreatitis severity if given early); antivenom; supportive care; prazosin 500 mcg repeated every 3-4 hours dramatically reduces morbidity from Mesobuthus tamulus envenomation in India

Serum triglycerides >1000 mg/dL (>11 mmol/L) cause acute pancreatitis through: release of toxic free fatty acids from triglyceride hydrolysis by pancreatic lipase (direct acinar cell injury); microvascular thrombosis in pancreatic capillaries from chylomicron hyperviscosity; typically associated with: type 1 hyperlipidaemia (familial lipoprotein lipase deficiency); type 5 hyperlipidaemia; secondary causes (untreated diabetes, hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, combined OCP, glucocorticoids, alcohol); management: INSULIN INFUSION (dramatically lowers triglycerides within hours — stimulates lipoprotein lipase); plasmapheresis for extreme hypertriglyceridaemia (>2000 mg/dL) resistant to insulin; fibrates and omega-3 fatty acids for secondary prevention

Elevated serum calcium (usually >3 mmol/L) → premature trypsinogen activation within pancreas (calcium activates trypsinogen directly); causes: primary hyperparathyroidism (most common cause of hypercalcaemia-induced pancreatitis — parathyroid adenoma or hyperplasia); malignancy-associated hypercalcaemia; sarcoidosis; vitamin D toxicity; treatment: IV fluids; bisphosphonates; treat underlying cause (parathyroidectomy for primary HPT)
Most preventable cause; prophylactic rectal indomethacin mandatory; aggressive IV fluid resuscitation peri-procedurally; pancreatic duct stenting in high-risk cases

Tropical chronic pancreatitis (see TYPE-03); Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm) migration into the pancreatic duct (ampullary obstruction); Clonorchis sinensis (liver fluke — biliary and pancreatic duct infestation); Typhoid fever (rare); organophosphate poisoning (acetylcholinesterase inhibition → excessive pancreatic stimulation)

symptoms.overview: The clinical presentation of pancreatitis varies significantly between acute and chronic forms. ACUTE PANCREATITIS presents suddenly and dramatically — severe upper abdominal pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and fever. CHRONIC PANCREATITIS presents more insidiously — chronic or recurrent epigastric pain, progressive weight loss from fat malabsorption (steatorrhoea), and ultimately diabetes. The hallmark pain of pancreatitis (both acute and chronic) is its retroperitoneal character — patients describe it as 'going through' or 'boring' from the front of the abdomen to the back, as if the pain is penetrating from the epigastrium straight through to the lumbar region. Sitting forward or leaning over reduces the pain (reduces tension on the inflamed retroperitoneal pancreas) — a characteristic posture of pancreatitis patients.

primary_symptoms.name: Epigastric Pain Radiating to the Back — Cardinal Symptom
primary_symptoms.description: The defining symptom of pancreatitis — severe, constant (not colicky), deep boring epigastric or upper abdominal pain radiating to the BACK (mid-back, T10-L1 level) or both flanks, sometimes described as a band-like sensation encircling the upper abdomen. ONSET: sudden in acute pancreatitis — may build rapidly over 30-60 minutes to peak intensity; gradual and persistent in chronic pancreatitis. SEVERITY: severe to excruciating in acute; variable in chronic (may be constant background ache with acute-on-chronic flares). POSTURE: CLASSIC POSTURE — leaning forward (sitting hunched, 'fetal position', 'praying position') partially relieves pain — a diagnostic characteristic distinguishing pancreatitis from other abdominal conditions. Lying supine significantly worsens pain (stretches the inflamed retroperitoneal pancreas against the spine). CHARACTER: constant, not colicky (no remissions), aching, boring, may be described as 'crushing' or 'knife in the back'. In chronic pancreatitis: the pain may follow meals (particularly fatty meals — which stimulate CCK and pancreatic secretion against a stenosed duct → ductal hypertension → pain); or may be constant without meal relationship in late-stage burnt-out disease.
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: The absence of abdominal rigidity (which is present in bowel perforation) and the pancreatic pain radiation pattern (back radiation) help distinguish pancreatitis from peptic ulcer perforation — though both cause severe upper abdominal pain and both can coexist

primary_symptoms.name: Nausea and Vomiting
primary_symptoms.description: Almost universal in acute pancreatitis — affecting >80% of patients. Vomiting is typically profuse, bile-stained, and does NOT relieve the pain (unlike peptic ulcer or biliary colic where vomiting may briefly reduce pain). Vomiting in pancreatitis results from: direct retroperitoneal inflammation stimulating visceral afferents; paralytic ileus from peritoneal irritation by inflammatory exudate; opiate analgesic administration; hyperacidaemia in some cases. Persistent vomiting prevents oral rehydration — central to the requirement for IV fluid therapy.
primary_symptoms.severity: Moderate to Severe in acute; Mild to Moderate in chronic

primary_symptoms.name: Fever
primary_symptoms.description: Low to moderate fever (38-39°C) is common in acute pancreatitis — from systemic release of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, TNF-alpha, IL-6 from activated macrophages and neutrophils). HIGH FEVER (>39.5°C) with rigors in a patient with acute pancreatitis suggests: infected pancreatic necrosis; ascending cholangitis (concurrent biliary obstruction); biliary sepsis. New fever developing after initial clinical improvement (5-7+ days into illness) in severe pancreatitis = INFECTED NECROSIS until proven otherwise — CT scan and CT-guided FNA required.
primary_symptoms.severity: Low-grade in mild; High fever indicates infected necrosis/sepsis

primary_symptoms.name: Steatorrhoea — Fatty Diarrhoea (Chronic Pancreatitis)
primary_symptoms.description: The cardinal gastrointestinal symptom of exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) — occurring in chronic pancreatitis when >90% of exocrine function is lost. Steatorrhoea presents as pale, bulky, greasy, foul-smelling stools that float in the toilet water (from fat content) and are difficult to flush (steatorrhoea — stool fat >7 g/day; normal <7 g/day). Patients may notice an oily film on the toilet water. Accompanying symptoms: bloating; flatulence; abdominal cramping; fat-soluble vitamin deficiency (Vitamins A, D, E, K — fat-soluble; malabsorption leads to night blindness, osteomalacia, neuropathy from Vitamin E deficiency, and bleeding tendency from Vitamin K deficiency).
primary_symptoms.note: Steatorrhoea is a LATE manifestation of chronic pancreatitis — it only appears when >90% of exocrine function is destroyed; earlier signs of chronic pancreatitis (pain, duct dilation) occur long before steatorrhoea

primary_symptoms.name: Weight Loss and Malnutrition
primary_symptoms.description: Progressive and often severe weight loss in chronic pancreatitis from multiple mechanisms: (1) Reduced food intake — eating exacerbates pain (postprandial pain — 'food fear'); (2) Fat malabsorption from EPI — steatorrhoea wastes calories; (3) Glucose intolerance and diabetes (FCPD) — increased catabolism; (4) Alcohol abuse contributing to nutritional neglect. In Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis: weight loss and malnutrition are often severe; patients may be extremely underweight (BMI 14-16). Nutritional rehabilitation is a cornerstone of TCP management.
primary_symptoms.severity: Moderate to Severe in chronic and TCP

primary_symptoms.name: Jaundice (Acute or Chronic — Obstruction)
primary_symptoms.description: Jaundice in pancreatitis results from: BILIARY OBSTRUCTION — a CBD stone causing simultaneous pancreatitis AND biliary obstruction (gallstone pancreatitis + cholangitis); the inflamed pancreatic head compressing the intrapancreatic portion of the CBD (inflammatory CBD stricture in acute pancreatitis — usually resolves); chronic fibrotic CBD stricture from chronic pancreatitis (particularly from pancreatic head inflammation); pancreatic pseudocyst or WON compressing the CBD; pancreatic cancer (important differential in chronic pancreatitis patients developing new painless jaundice — urgent investigation). Jaundice with fever and RUQ pain = cholangitis = EMERGENCY.
primary_symptoms.clinical_importance: New onset jaundice in a patient with established chronic pancreatitis is an ALARM FEATURE for pancreatic cancer — urgent EUS and CT staging required

primary_symptoms.name: Hyperglycaemia and Diabetes (Type 3c — Pancreatogenic Diabetes)
primary_symptoms.description: Endocrine insufficiency from islet cell destruction — occurring in 20-30% of chronic pancreatitis patients and in 30-60% of Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis patients (Fibrocalculous Pancreatic Diabetes — FCPD). Type 3c diabetes (pancreatogenic diabetes) is distinct from Type 1 and Type 2 diabetes: loss of BOTH alpha cells (glucagon) AND beta cells (insulin) causes unstable, brittle glycaemia; absence of glucagon counterregulation makes hypoglycaemia particularly dangerous and difficult to detect (hypoglycaemia unawareness); patients often require insulin but have very low daily insulin requirements from concomitant malabsorption reducing glucose load; initial polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss are the presenting features.
primary_symptoms.india_specific: FCPD in TCP patients is often severe, brittle, and difficult to manage; ketoacidosis is uncommon (some residual C-peptide); hypoglycaemia is the more dangerous acute complication; poor glycaemic control accelerates diabetic complications (retinopathy, nephropathy, neuropathy) in young TCP patients

secondary_symptoms: Abdominal distension and paralytic ileus — from retroperitoneal inflammation; severe acute pancreatitis; absent bowel sounds

Grey Turner's sign (flank bruising — bluish-purple discolouration) — retroperitoneal haemorrhage tracking along fascial planes to flanks; present in <3% of acute pancreatitis; indicates haemorrhagic necrotising pancreatitis; very poor prognostic sign
Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising — bluish discolouration around the navel) — blood tracking from retroperitoneum to umbilicus via falciform ligament; similarly rare and prognostically ominous
Tachycardia and hypotension — from systemic inflammatory response and fluid sequestration ('third spacing') into retroperitoneum and peritoneum; early sign of moderate-severe acute pancreatitis

Respiratory distress — ARDS (Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome) complicating severe acute pancreatitis; dyspnoea; hypoxaemia; bilateral infiltrates on chest X-ray; caused by pancreatic phospholipase A2 attacking pulmonary surfactant

Pleural effusion — left-sided or bilateral; from pancreatic enzyme-rich fluid tracking superiorly via lymphatics; amylase-rich pleural fluid is pathognomonic of pancreatic pleural effusion; may indicate pancreatic duct disruption in chronic pancreatitis
Pancreatic ascites — enzyme-rich (very high amylase) peritoneal fluid from pancreatic duct disruption; indicates duct tear or pseudocyst rupture

Tetany — rare; from hypocalcaemia (calcium chelated by released fatty acids — saponification of peripancreatic fat by pancreatic lipase); low serum calcium (<2 mmol/L) in severe acute pancreatitis is a poor prognostic feature (Ranson's criterion)
warning_signs_severe_pancreatitis: Tachycardia >120 bpm not improving with IV fluids — possible systemic inflammatory response or occult haemorrhage
Oxygen saturation <94% on room air — early ARDS from pancreatitis
Oliguria (urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr) despite adequate IV fluids — acute kidney injury
Rising serum creatinine >170 mcmol/L — renal failure
Confusion or altered consciousness — septic encephalopathy or severe electrolyte disturbance
New fever (>39°C) after initial improvement at 5-7 days — infected necrosis (not 'spontaneous fever from pancreatitis' — new fever always requires CT and consideration of FNA)
Gas bubbles in pancreatic area on CT — INFECTED NECROSIS — immediate antibiotics and step-up drainage
Grey Turner's or Cullen's sign — haemorrhagic pancreatitis — extreme severity

medical_history: Onset and character of pain — sudden vs gradual; epigastric location; back radiation; postural modification (sitting forward relieves pain — characteristic); duration; severity (NRS/10)
Dietary history immediately before onset — last meal; fatty meal? Large meal? Restaurant food? — biliary aetiology suspicion
Alcohol history — amount (g/day); frequency; duration; last drink; type of alcohol; binge drinking pattern vs sustained heavy use
Smoking history — pack-years; current or past smoker (synergistic with alcohol for chronic pancreatitis)
Medication history — ALL medications including herbal preparations; azathioprine; 6-MP; valproate; tetracyclines; GLP-1 agonists; oestrogens; diuretics; statins
Previous episodes — prior pancreatitis (acute or chronic); number of prior hospitalisations; what investigations were performed previously; cause identified?
Gallstone history — previous gallstone diagnosis; symptoms of biliary colic; previous cholecystectomy (if yes — gallstone as current cause unlikely but CBD stones still possible)
ERCP history — recent ERCP within 72 hours (post-ERCP pancreatitis)
Abdominal trauma — recent injury; steering wheel impact; sports injury
Family history — pancreatitis; pancreatic cancer; cystic fibrosis; hereditary pancreatitis (PRSS1 mutations)
Diet and nutritional history (for TCP assessment) — cassava (tapioca) consumption; malnutrition in childhood; rural South India origin; young age + non-alcoholic + pancreatic calcifications = TCP
Diabetes history — recent onset of diabetes; polyuria, polydipsia; HbA1c; insulin use (new onset diabetes in chronic pancreatitis patient = rule out pancreatic cancer)
Lipid profile — known hypertriglyceridaemia; fasting lipid history; diabetes-associated dyslipidaemia
Calcium history — hypercalcaemia symptoms (bone pain, stones, groans, moans); hyperparathyroidism; vitamin D supplements in high dose
Scorpion sting history — in Maharashtra, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Tamil Nadu — ask specifically about scorpion sting 12-48 hours before onset
physical_examination: Vital signs — temperature (fever = infection or SIRS); heart rate (tachycardia = SIRS, dehydration, sepsis); blood pressure (hypotension = severe pancreatitis, septic shock); respiratory rate and SpO2 (hypoxaemia = ARDS, pleural effusion); urine output monitoring (oliguria = AKI)

General appearance — distress level; posture (hunched forward = characteristic pancreatitis posture); pallor (anaemia from chronic disease or haemorrhagic pancreatitis); jaundice (biliary obstruction); nutritional status (wasting in chronic pancreatitis — particularly TCP patients)
INSPECTION: Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising — haemorrhagic pancreatitis); Grey Turner's sign (flank bruising); abdominal distension (ileus, ascites); visible peristalsis (obstruction)

PALPATION: Epigastric tenderness (most prominent finding — often severe guarding and voluntary rigidity; peritonism indicates more severe disease; epigastric mass = pseudocyst); rebound tenderness (peritoneal irritation); hepatomegaly or splenomegaly (portal/splenic vein thrombosis in chronic pancreatitis — important complication); Courvoisier's sign: painless palpable distended gallbladder + jaundice = pancreatic head mass (cancer) NOT pancreatitis (gallstone obstruction contracts the gallbladder)
PERCUSSION: Shifting dullness (ascites — pancreatic); dullness at lung bases (pleural effusion — left > right in pancreatitis)
AUSCULTATION: Absent or markedly reduced bowel sounds (ileus from retroperitoneal inflammation); reduced air entry at left base (pleural effusion)
Skin — xanthomata or xanthelasma (hyperlipidaemia-associated pancreatitis); jaundice scleral assessment; lipemic retinalis on fundoscopy (gross hypertriglyceridaemia — milky/creamy plasma)

Signs of chronic liver disease — spider naevi, palmar erythema, caput medusae (portal hypertension from splenic vein thrombosis in chronic pancreatitis); gynaecomastia; testicular atrophy (alcoholic chronic pancreatitis)

Signs of scorpion envenomation — if relevant history: piloerection; diaphoresis; tachyarrhythmia; hypertension followed by hypotension; localised wound (often on hands/feet); sympathetic overactivation

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Lipase — Gold Standard Biochemical Diagnosis
diagnostic_tests.description: The PREFERRED biochemical test for diagnosing acute pancreatitis — superior to serum amylase in sensitivity (80-100%) and specificity (85-99%). Serum lipase rises 4-8 hours after acute pancreatitis onset, peaks at 24 hours, and remains elevated for 7-14 days (much longer than amylase — 3-5 days). Lipase is produced almost exclusively by the pancreatic acini — making it more specific than amylase (which is produced by salivary glands, bowel, ovaries, and fallopian tubes — these non-pancreatic sources can raise amylase without pancreatitis). The diagnostic threshold is ≥3× upper limit of normal (≥3× ULN).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose acute pancreatitis; the height of elevation does NOT correlate with disease severity
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Lipase ≥3× ULN = acute pancreatitis diagnosis (combined with clinical features); normal: <60-80 U/L depending on laboratory; ACG guidelines: lipase >3× ULN is the biochemical diagnostic criterion for acute pancreatitis
diagnostic_tests.note: Lipase elevation does NOT correlate with severity — a mildly ill patient can have extremely high lipase; a severely ill patient with pancreatic burn-out may have nearly normal lipase

diagnostic_tests.description: Rises rapidly within 2-12 hours of acute pancreatitis onset but returns to normal within 3-5 days (much earlier than lipase — thus lipase is preferred for patients presenting late). The diagnostic threshold is ≥3× ULN. FALSE POSITIVES for elevated amylase are important: bowel ischaemia; perforated peptic ulcer; salivary gland disease; parotitis; renal failure (reduced amylase clearance); macroamylasaemia; ectopic pregnancy; ovarian tumours.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Historical gold standard for acute pancreatitis diagnosis; now superseded by lipase at most centres
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Amylase ≥3× ULN = supports acute pancreatitis diagnosis

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Contrast-Enhanced CT Scan (CECT) Abdomen — Gold Standard for Severity Assessment
diagnostic_tests.description: The definitive imaging modality for assessing severity, local complications, and necrosis in acute pancreatitis. IV contrast is essential — areas of non-enhancement after contrast = pancreatic necrosis (areas of ischaemic acinar destruction). CT should NOT be performed within the first 48-72 hours of onset (pancreatic necrosis takes time to declare — early CT may underestimate extent of necrosis and is not useful for immediate management of mild pancreatitis). INDICATIONS for CT: all patients with moderately severe or severe pancreatitis; patients not improving at 72 hours; suspected infected necrosis (new fever, rising inflammatory markers after initial improvement); baseline prior to any intervention.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Quantify necrosis extent (CT Severity Index / Balthazar score); identify local complications (fluid collections, pseudocysts, WON); detect complications (portal/splenic vein thrombosis, pseudoaneurysm, ascites); guide interventional drainage; detect infected necrosis (gas within collection); pancreatic cancer surveillance in chronic pancreatitis
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Balthazar CT Grade (A-E) + Necrosis Score = CTSI 0-10; non-enhanced pancreatic parenchyma on IV contrast = necrosis; gas within collection = infected necrosis (pathognomonic)
diagnostic_tests.timing: Perform at 48-72 hours in moderate-severe pancreatitis; not routine in mild pancreatitis (adds radiation, cost, and IV contrast risk without changing management)

diagnostic_tests.description: The FIRST-LINE IMAGING INVESTIGATION for all acute pancreatitis — to assess for GALLSTONES (the most common cause) and biliary dilation. Ultrasound is NOT sensitive for detecting pancreatic necrosis or early pancreatic changes (overlying bowel gas obscures the pancreas in most acute pancreatitis patients) — CT is required for severity assessment. Ultrasound findings in acute pancreatitis: gallstones in gallbladder; dilated CBD (>6 mm = possible CBD stone causing obstruction); oedematous pancreas (when visible — appears enlarged and hypoechoic); peripancreatic fluid; pseudocysts (rounded, well-defined, anechoic).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify gallstones and biliary aetiology (performed in ALL acute pancreatitis patients); screen for biliary obstruction; detect pseudocysts in chronic pancreatitis; guided aspiration of collections
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Gallstones in GB + acute pancreatitis = gallstone pancreatitis aetiology; dilated CBD = biliary obstruction; pericholecystic fluid + thickened GB wall = concomitant acute cholecystitis

diagnostic_tests.description: Detailed non-invasive visualisation of the entire biliary and pancreatic ductal system — particularly important in chronic pancreatitis evaluation. MRCP superiority over CT in pancreatitis: (1) Characterises ductal anatomy in chronic pancreatitis (strictures, dilation patterns, ductal stones, pancreas divisum); (2) Detects CBD stones before ERCP; (3) Identifies pancreatic duct disruption (causing pseudocysts or ascites); (4) Better characterisation of WON contents (solid vs liquid — guides drainage approach); (5) No radiation. In CHRONIC PANCREATITIS: MRCP shows the 'chain-of-lakes' appearance (alternating dilations and strictures) or 'beaded duct' pattern; demonstrates large intraductal stones (TCP); reveals complete ductal anatomy before surgical drainage procedures (Puestow operation).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Evaluate pancreatic and biliary ducts; detect CBD stones; characterise chronic pancreatitis ductal changes; TCP assessment (duct dilation and stones); pre-ERCP and pre-surgical planning; pancreatic duct disruption

diagnostic_tests.description: A high-frequency ultrasound probe on an endoscope positioned in the duodenum or stomach provides ultra-high-resolution pancreatic and biliary imaging. EUS superiority: detects pancreatic microlithiasis (tiny stones <2 mm not visible on transabdominal ultrasound — the most common cause of 'idiopathic' recurrent acute pancreatitis); detects early chronic pancreatitis changes (parenchymal and ductal features — Rosemont criteria); characterises cystic lesions; guides FNA of necrotic collections; guides endoscopic drainage (EUS-guided transmural drainage of pseudocysts and WON — EUS identifies the optimal puncture site and avoids intervening blood vessels).
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Investigate 'idiopathic' acute pancreatitis (detect microlithiasis, occult CBD stones, SOD); diagnose early chronic pancreatitis (Rosemont criteria); characterise cystic pancreatic lesions; guide drainage of pseudocysts and WON; detect early pancreatic cancer in chronic pancreatitis surveillance

diagnostic_tests.description: The most widely used non-invasive test for exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) — measuring the concentration of elastase-1 enzyme (produced exclusively by pancreatic acinar cells) in stool. Human pancreatic elastase-1 is stable through gut transit and concentrated approximately 5× in stool vs duodenal juice — allowing accurate measurement even without pancreatic stimulation. Sensitivity: 73-100% for moderate-severe EPI; 63% for mild EPI.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose exocrine pancreatic insufficiency in chronic pancreatitis; determine when to start PERT; assess severity of EPI; screen for EPI in TCP patients (where it develops early due to severe ductal obstruction)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: FE-1 >200 mcg/g stool = normal exocrine function; 100-200 mcg/g = mild-moderate EPI; <100 mcg/g = severe EPI — PERT mandatory; false low results with diarrhoea (dilution effect — collect formed stool only)
diagnostic_tests.alternatives: 72-hour faecal fat quantification (gold standard for fat malabsorption — labour intensive; 7g/day = steatorrhoea); secretin-stimulated MRCP (direct ductal flow measurement — very sensitive for early EPI; used at specialist centres)

diagnostic_tests.description: CRP is the most important PROGNOSTIC marker in acute pancreatitis at 48 hours — when the inflammatory cytokine cascade has had time to manifest. CRP >150 mg/L at 48 hours has sensitivity of 80% and specificity of 76% for predicting severe acute pancreatitis. Peak CRP at 72 hours further refines prognostication.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Predict severity at 48-72 hours; guide ICU admission decisions; monitor response to treatment
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: CRP >150 mg/L at 48h = moderately severe/severe pancreatitis prediction; CRP <150 mg/L at 48h + BISAP ≤2 = likely mild pancreatitis

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Serum Triglycerides and Fasting Lipid Profile
diagnostic_tests.description: MUST be measured in all acute pancreatitis patients where aetiology is unclear — hypertriglyceridaemia is a treatable cause. A sample from a hypertriglyceridaemia patient's blood typically appears MILKY or CREAMY (lipaemic serum — grossly visible when triglycerides >1000 mg/dL). Importantly, gross hypertriglyceridaemia causes FALSELY LOW serum amylase (dilution effect from icteric/lipaemic sample) — pancreatitis from hypertriglyceridaemia may have misleadingly low or near-normal amylase; USE LIPASE instead or use urine amylase.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify hypertriglyceridaemia as aetiology; guide treatment (insulin infusion; fibrates); prevent recurrence
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: Triglycerides >1000 mg/dL (>11 mmol/L) = risk factor; >2000 mg/dL = high risk; consider plasmapheresis

diagnostic_tests.description: Hypercalcaemia (>3 mmol/L) can cause acute pancreatitis; hypocalcaemia occurs as a COMPLICATION of severe acute pancreatitis (calcium chelated by released fatty acids — saponification). Both are clinically important to detect. Low calcium <2 mmol/L in severe pancreatitis is a Ranson's prognostic criterion and requires IV calcium gluconate replacement.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify hypercalcaemia as aetiology; detect hypocalcaemia complication (tetany risk); Ranson scoring

diagnostic_tests.description: Serum IgG4 is elevated in Type 1 autoimmune pancreatitis (AIP) — an IgG4-related disease. IgG4 >2× ULN (>2.8 g/L) is highly specific (>95%) for AIP Type 1 — though false positives occur in pancreatic cancer and primary sclerosing cholangitis. IgG4 is NORMAL in Type 2 AIP. Sensitivity of IgG4 for AIP Type 1 is only 70-75% — 25-30% of confirmed AIP has normal IgG4.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Screen for autoimmune pancreatitis Type 1; aid in differentiating AIP from pancreatic cancer (critical differential)
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: IgG4 >2× ULN (>2.8 g/L): highly specific for AIP Type 1; IgG4 >4× ULN: nearly diagnostic

diagnostic_tests.test_name: CT-Guided Fine Needle Aspiration (FNA) of Necrotic Collection
diagnostic_tests.description: CT-guided percutaneous insertion of a fine needle into a necrotic collection to aspirate material for Gram stain and culture — confirming infected vs sterile necrosis. This distinction is critical because: STERILE NECROSIS is managed conservatively without antibiotics (antibiotics provide no benefit for sterile necrosis and drive resistance); INFECTED NECROSIS requires antibiotics AND drainage. FNA should be performed when: clinical deterioration with fever 5-7+ days after onset; gas in necrotic collection on CT (pathognomonic of infection — FNA not required in this case — treat as infected); clinical suspicion of infection.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Confirm infected vs sterile necrosis; guide antibiotic decisions; identify organisms for targeted therapy

diagnostic_tests.test_name: Genetic Testing — SPINK1, PRSS1, CFTR, CTRC
diagnostic_tests.description: Genetic testing for hereditary and tropical pancreatitis susceptibility genes — recommended in: young patients (<35 years) with recurrent acute or chronic pancreatitis without alcoholic or gallstone cause; TCP patients (SPINK1 N34S mutation testing); family history of pancreatitis; unexplained childhood pancreatitis; patients being considered for total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation (TP-IAT). In India: SPINK1 N34S mutation testing is available at AIIMS Delhi, PGI Chandigarh, CMC Vellore, and several major medical centres.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Identify genetic cause of pancreatitis; guide counselling; family screening; surgical decision-making
diagnostic_tests.india_note: SPINK1 N34S is the most clinically important genetic variant for Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis in India — found in 25-40% of TCP patients; heterozygous for SPINK1 with normal CFTR represents a significant risk

diagnostic_tests.test_name: HbA1c and C-Peptide — Pancreatogenic Diabetes Assessment
diagnostic_tests.description: Essential in all chronic pancreatitis patients — to assess for Type 3c pancreatogenic diabetes. HbA1c reflects average glycaemia over 3 months; C-peptide measures endogenous insulin secretory capacity (produced equimolarly with insulin by beta cells). In FCPD/Type 3c diabetes: C-peptide is very LOW (but often detectable — unlike Type 1 diabetes where C-peptide is completely absent); absence of ketoacidosis in severe hyperglycaemia; very low insulin requirements with significant hypoglycaemia risk.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Diagnose pancreatogenic diabetes; classify diabetes type (Type 3c vs Type 1 vs Type 2 — important for management); assess residual beta cell function (C-peptide); guide insulin therapy
diagnostic_tests.key_metric: HbA1c >48 mmol/mol (6.5%) = diabetes diagnostic criterion; C-peptide <0.2 nmol/L = severe beta cell deficiency

diagnostic_tests.description: CA 19-9 monitoring in chronic pancreatitis patients for pancreatic cancer surveillance — particularly in TCP and hereditary pancreatitis (very high cancer risk). CA 19-9 is NOT a screening test (insufficient sensitivity — 80% sensitivity; specificity — elevated in biliary obstruction, cholangitis, pancreatitis flares); but a rising CA 19-9 in a chronic pancreatitis patient with new symptoms (new pain, weight loss, jaundice) warrants urgent EUS and CT. Baseline CA 19-9 should be established in all chronic pancreatitis patients.
diagnostic_tests.purpose: Cancer surveillance in high-risk chronic pancreatitis; monitor for cancer development in TCP, hereditary pancreatitis, AIP

medicines.note: Treatment of pancreatitis is primarily SUPPORTIVE for acute episodes (fluid resuscitation is the most critical intervention) and SUBSTITUTIVE for chronic disease (pancreatic enzyme replacement therapy — PERT — and insulin for loss of exocrine and endocrine function). Antibiotics are used ONLY for documented infected necrosis — NOT prophylactically. The role of nutrition has shifted dramatically: early enteral nutrition (nasogastric or nasojejunal feeding within 24-48 hours) is now strongly preferred over prolonged NPO and TPN — maintaining gut barrier integrity, reducing bacterial translocation, and reducing infectious complications.
treatment_principles: 1. IV FLUID RESUSCITATION is the single most critical and most evidence-based intervention for acute pancreatitis — 'fluid is medicine'; Ringer's Lactate preferred over normal saline; aggressive early resuscitation within the first 24-48 hours reduces organ failure and mortality
2. ANALGESIA: adequate analgesia is essential — undertreated pain increases sympathetic activation, worsening outcome; opioids are appropriate and safe; NSAIDs are useful adjuncts

3. EARLY ENTERAL NUTRITION within 24-48 hours (whenever tolerated) is superior to prolonged NPO and TPN — reduces infectious complications by maintaining gut mucosal barrier; nasogastric route is safe for mild-moderate pancreatitis; nasojejunal route for patients who cannot tolerate nasogastric

4. ANTIBIOTICS ONLY FOR DOCUMENTED INFECTED NECROSIS — never prophylactic antibiotics for acute pancreatitis (no evidence of benefit; drives resistance; increases Candida risk); meropenem or imipenem for infected necrosis
5. PERT (Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy) is the cornerstone of chronic pancreatitis management for exocrine insufficiency — given WITH EVERY MEAL AND SNACK
6. INSULIN for Type 3c diabetes — handle with extreme caution given hypoglycaemia unawareness and absent glucagon counterregulation
7. ALCOHOL AND TOBACCO CESSATION are the only disease-modifying interventions for alcoholic chronic pancreatitis — no medication substitutes for complete abstinence

categories.category_name: IV Fluid Resuscitation — THE MOST CRITICAL ACUTE TREATMENT
categories.purpose: Replace massive fluid losses from vomiting and 'third spacing' (fluid sequestration into retroperitoneum, peritoneum, and bowel lumen from inflammatory vasodilation and capillary leak); maintain pancreatic microcirculation to prevent ischaemia and necrosis; reduce SIRS progression; reduce organ failure risk.

medicines.name: Ringer's Lactate (Hartmann's Solution) — Preferred IV Fluid
medicines.dosage: MILD ACUTE PANCREATITIS: 250-500 mL/hour for first 12-24 hours; total 3-5 litres in first 24 hours; reassess every 4-6 hours; target: urine output >0.5 mL/kg/hour; heart rate <100 bpm; no significant thirst; BUN declining. MODERATE-SEVERE: 500 mL bolus then 250-500 mL/hour with close monitoring; may require 5-10 litres in first 24 hours; reassess every 1-2 hours in ICU
medicines.use_case: The CORNERSTONE of acute pancreatitis treatment — aggressive early Ringer's Lactate resuscitation in the first 24-48 hours; the WATERFALL RCT (2021) and URGE TRIAL demonstrated Ringer's Lactate superiority over normal saline: reduces SIRS rate (35% → 23%), reduces moderate-severe pancreatitis rate, reduces organ failure
medicines.mechanism: Ringer's Lactate contains lactate which is metabolised to bicarbonate — corrects metabolic acidosis from SIRS; contains potassium and calcium at physiological concentrations; anti-inflammatory property of lactate reduces NF-κB activation in acinar cells; avoids hyperchloraemic acidosis from normal saline
medicines.monitoring: Vital signs every 1-4 hours; urine output hourly (catheterise in severe pancreatitis); BUN (trend — falling BUN = adequate resuscitation); haematocrit (falling from initial haemoconcentration = good resuscitation); clinical reassessment for fluid overload (bilateral crackles, worsening oxygenation — especially in elderly and cardiac disease)
medicines.caution: Avoid over-resuscitation — overly aggressive fluid resuscitation in delayed presentations causes abdominal compartment syndrome, worsening ARDS, and increased mortality; reassess fluid need at 24-48 hours

categories.purpose: Adequate pain control — essential for patient comfort, reduction of sympathetic activation, and reduction of splanchnic vasoconstriction that worsens pancreatic ischaemia.

medicines.name: Diclofenac / Ketorolac (IV/IM NSAIDs)
brand_examples: Diclofenac: Voveran, Voltaren IV; Ketorolac: Ketanov, Toradol
medicines.dosage: Diclofenac 75 mg IV over 30-60 min every 8-12 hours; Ketorolac 30 mg IV/IM every 6 hours (maximum 5 days)
medicines.use_case: Initial analgesia for mild-moderate pancreatitis pain; anti-inflammatory component; combine with opioids for moderate-severe pain; IV paracetamol 1g every 6 hours as opioid-sparing adjunct
medicines.caution: Avoid in AKI (renal impairment — NSAIDs reduce renal perfusion); avoid with active GI bleeding; limit to 5 days maximum

medicines.name: Morphine (IV PCA) / Pethidine
medicines.form: IV infusion; IV patient-controlled analgesia (PCA); IM
medicines.dosage: Morphine: 2-4 mg IV every 4 hours (titrate to pain control); PCA: 1 mg/actuation with 5-minute lockout; Pethidine: 50-100 mg IM every 4-6 hours
medicines.use_case: Moderate to severe acute pancreatitis pain requiring hospital admission; the historical concern that morphine causes sphincter of Oddi spasm worsening pancreatitis is OUTDATED — morphine is safe in pancreatitis; pethidine has no proven advantage and norpethidine accumulates causing seizures with repeated dosing
medicines.note: Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia (IV paracetamol + NSAID + low-dose opioid) reduces opioid side effects (nausea, constipation, respiratory depression, ileus)

medicines.name: Tramadol
medicines.dosage: 50-100 mg IV/IM every 6-8 hours; 50-100 mg oral every 6-8 hours
medicines.use_case: Moderate pain; useful oral agent; safer than opioids for oral analgesia in mild pancreatitis

medicines.name: IV Paracetamol
medicines.dosage: 1g IV over 15 minutes every 6 hours
medicines.use_case: Opioid-sparing multimodal analgesia; safe in all patients including those with renal impairment (where NSAIDs are contraindicated)

medicines.name: Epidural Analgesia (Thoracic Epidural)
medicines.description: Thoracic epidural catheter (T6-T10 level) providing continuous infusion of local anaesthetic (bupivacaine) with or without opioid — for intractable severe acute pancreatitis pain. Provides excellent analgesia; also improves pancreatic microcirculation (sympathetic blockade causes splanchnic vasodilation); reduces SIRS response; considered in ICU patients with severe pain not controlled by IV analgesics
medicines.use_case: Severe acute pancreatitis with refractory pain; ICU patients; reduces systemic opioid requirements

categories.purpose: Provide adequate calories and protein to prevent malnutrition, support immune function, maintain gut mucosal barrier (preventing bacterial translocation), and promote pancreatic rest and healing.
categories.nutrition_principles: EARLY ENTERAL NUTRITION (within 24-48 hours) is now the standard of care for all acute pancreatitis requiring hospital admission — early enteral nutrition reduces: infectious complications (by maintaining gut mucosal barrier and competitive exclusion of gut bacteria); organ failure; need for surgery; length of hospital stay; vs parenteral nutrition (TPN): enteral nutrition is safer, cheaper, maintains gut integrity, and has superior outcomes

medicines.name: Nasogastric (NG) Tube Enteral Nutrition — Mild to Moderate AP
medicines.description: Polymeric standard enteral feed delivered via nasogastric tube; safe for mild and moderate acute pancreatitis — the stomach can be used (nasogastric route is as safe as nasojejunal for mild-moderate pancreatitis per PYTHON trial); used when patient cannot tolerate adequate oral intake
medicines.dosage: Start at 20-25 mL/hour; increase to target rate over 24-48 hours based on tolerance; target 25-30 kcal/kg/day; 1.2-1.5 g protein/kg/day
medicines.use_case: Patients unable to eat adequately (pain, nausea, vomiting) who have mild-moderate pancreatitis and functioning gut

medicines.name: Nasojejunal (NJ) Tube Enteral Nutrition — Severe AP and Gastroparesis
medicines.description: Enteral nutrition delivered into the distal jejunum (past the Treitz ligament) via a post-pyloric feeding tube — placed endoscopically or fluoroscopically; used for: severe acute pancreatitis; patients with paralytic ileus limiting gastric tolerance; patients who do not tolerate nasogastric feeding; gastroparesis
medicines.dosage: Semi-elemental or elemental formula (hydrolysed protein); start 10-15 mL/hour; titrate to 30-35 kcal/kg/day
medicines.note: Post-pyloric position minimises pancreatic stimulation in severe pancreatitis (though recent evidence suggests the pancreatic stimulation difference between NG and NJ feeding is clinically not significant in mild-moderate pancreatitis)

medicines.name: Total Parenteral Nutrition (TPN) — When Enteral Route Not Possible
medicines.description: IV nutrition via central venous catheter — ONLY when enteral route is completely impossible (e.g., bowel obstruction, intestinal fistula, complete gut failure); associated with significantly higher infectious complications (line infections, gut bacterial translocation) and should be avoided unless absolutely necessary
medicines.use_case: Short-gut syndrome; complete intestinal obstruction; severe WON with gastric outlet obstruction; as BRIDGE while enteral access is being established; NOT routine in acute pancreatitis

categories.purpose: Targeted antibiotic therapy for CONFIRMED INFECTED PANCREATIC NECROSIS — NOT prophylactic use.
categories.critical_evidence: Multiple RCTs and meta-analyses have conclusively shown that PROPHYLACTIC ANTIBIOTICS in acute pancreatitis DO NOT reduce infected necrosis, organ failure, or mortality — and increase Candida infection risk; all major international guidelines (ACG, IAP, BSG, Indian guidelines) recommend AGAINST prophylactic antibiotics for acute pancreatitis

medicines.name: Meropenem — First-Line for Infected Pancreatic Necrosis
medicines.dosage: 1-2g IV every 8 hours; for infected necrosis — typically 14-21 day course guided by clinical response and culture results
medicines.use_case: INFECTED PANCREATIC NECROSIS — confirmed by: CT showing gas within necrotic collection (pathognomonic); CT-FNA with positive Gram stain or culture; clinical deterioration with new fever >5 days into illness with rising WBC and CRP not responding to supportive care
medicines.mechanism: Carbapenem — broadest-spectrum beta-lactam; excellent penetration into pancreatic necrotic tissue (penetration index ~40% of serum levels — superior to most other antibiotics); active against: Gram-negative enteric bacteria (E. coli, Klebsiella, Pseudomonas), Gram-positive cocci, and anaerobes
medicines.note: Add fluconazole or micafungin if Candida identified in culture (particularly in patients on prolonged broad-spectrum antibiotics)

medicines.name: Imipenem-Cilastatin — Alternative First-Line
medicines.dosage: 500 mg IV every 6 hours
medicines.use_case: Alternative to meropenem for infected pancreatic necrosis; equally effective pancreatic tissue penetration

categories.category_name: Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT) — Exocrine Insufficiency
categories.purpose: Replace the endogenous pancreatic digestive enzymes (lipase, amylase, protease) lost from exocrine pancreatic insufficiency (EPI) in chronic pancreatitis — restoring fat, protein, and carbohydrate digestion; eliminating steatorrhoea; improving caloric absorption; correcting malnutrition; improving quality of life.
key_principles: TAKE WITH EVERY MEAL AND SNACK — NOT before or after food; capsules taken at the start of, during, or immediately after each meal/snack for maximum mixing with food in the duodenum
DOSE IS FLEXIBLE — adjust based on symptom response (stool consistency, frequency, presence of steatorrhoea, weight gain); start with standard dose and up-titrate if symptoms persist

ADD PPI (omeprazole 20 mg once daily) — gastric acid rapidly inactivates exogenous pancreatic enzymes in the duodenum; PPI reduces acid secretion and raises duodenal pH, protecting PERT enzymes and extending their activity
ADEQUATE DOSE — many patients are underdosed; insufficient PERT dose does not treat EPI; minimum 40,000 IU lipase per main meal

ENTERIC-COATED MICROSPHERES — the preferred formulation; microspheres (1-2 mm diameter) mix with food in the stomach and the enteric coating protects them from gastric acid inactivation until they reach the duodenum and dissolve at pH >5

medicines.name: Pancreatin — Enteric-Coated Minimiccrospheres (Pancrelipase)
medicines.form: Enteric-coated microsphere capsule; capsules can be opened and microspheres sprinkled on food for patients who cannot swallow capsules
medicines.dosage: STARTING DOSE: 25,000-40,000 IU lipase per main meal; 10,000-25,000 IU per snack. TITRATION: if steatorrhoea persists — increase dose; maximum 80,000-100,000 IU per meal (above this rarely provides additional benefit); TYPICAL DAILY DOSE for severe EPI: 50,000-80,000 IU × 3 main meals = 150,000-240,000 IU lipase per day
medicines.mechanism: Porcine-derived pancreatin mixture containing lipase (primary enzyme for fat digestion — steatorrhoea is primarily from lipase deficiency), amylase (carbohydrate), and protease (protein); enteric coating (methacrylic acid copolymer) protects from gastric acid; dissolves in duodenum at pH >5-5.5
medicines.monitoring: Symptom response (stool normalisation — formed, not greasy, not floating; reduced frequency); weight gain; fat-soluble vitamin levels (A, D, E, K); faecal elastase (does not change with PERT — reflects endogenous production); HbA1c for FCPD
side_effects: GI symptoms (nausea, abdominal discomfort) at very high doses
Fibrosing colonopathy (rare — only at extremely high doses >10,000 IU lipase/kg/day; primarily described in cystic fibrosis children on excessively high doses)
medicines.india_availability: Creon and Panzytrat available at major pharmacies in India; cost Rs 15-30 per capsule; a significant cost burden for TCP patients — government-subsidised PERT procurement is urgently needed for TCP patients from low-income backgrounds

categories.purpose: Replace fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K) malabsorbed in exocrine pancreatic insufficiency — critical to prevent serious complications of chronic deficiency.

medicines.name: Vitamin D3 (Cholecalciferol)
medicines.dosage: Maintenance: 1,000-2,000 IU daily; Deficiency treatment: 60,000 IU weekly × 8-12 weeks; Monitor: serum 25-OH Vitamin D (target 30-50 ng/mL)
medicines.use_case: Universal in chronic pancreatitis with EPI; osteomalacia and osteoporosis prevention; very high deficiency prevalence in chronic pancreatitis (80-90%) due to fat malabsorption

medicines.name: Vitamin K (Phytomenadione)
medicines.dosage: Oral: 10 mg weekly (monitor PT/INR); IV/IM if severe deficiency or unable to absorb orally
medicines.use_case: Bleeding tendency from Vitamin K deficiency (coagulopathy — elevated PT/INR); Vitamin K required for clotting factors II, VII, IX, X

medicines.name: Vitamin E (Tocopherol)
medicines.dosage: 400 IU daily
medicines.use_case: Deficiency causes peripheral neuropathy; antioxidant properties may reduce oxidative stress-related pancreatic inflammation

medicines.name: Vitamin A (Retinol)
medicines.dosage: 5,000-10,000 IU daily (oral)
medicines.use_case: Night blindness; immune function; skin; monitor levels to avoid toxicity

categories.purpose: Chronic pancreatitis pain is one of the most difficult pain syndromes in medicine — often severe, constant, multimechanistic, and requires a multimodal pharmacological and interventional approach.
