categories.pain_mechanisms: Ductal hypertension (obstruction from stones/strictures — relieved by drainage procedures); neuro-inflammation (activation and upregulation of pancreatic nociceptors — peripheral sensitisation); central sensitisation (spinal cord and brain sensitisation — explains pain persistence even after successful decompression); acute-on-chronic episodes

medicines.name: Paracetamol (Step 1 Analgesic)
medicines.dosage: 500-1000 mg every 6-8 hours (maximum 4g/day; 2g/day in liver impairment)
medicines.use_case: First-line analgesic for chronic pancreatitis pain; non-opioid; minimal GI side effects; safe long-term

medicines.name: Tramadol — Weak Opioid
medicines.dosage: 50-100 mg every 6-8 hours (maximum 400 mg/day); modified-release: 100-200 mg twice daily
medicines.use_case: Step 2 analgesic for chronic pancreatitis pain not controlled by paracetamol alone; weaker opioid effect; serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibition adds central analgesic benefit

medicines.name: Pregabalin — Neuromodulator for Chronic Pain
medicines.dosage: 75-150 mg twice daily; titrate slowly upward over weeks; maximum 300-600 mg/day in divided doses
medicines.use_case: Central sensitisation in chronic pancreatitis; RCT (Olesen et al., Lancet 2011): pregabalin significantly reduces chronic pancreatitis pain vs placebo; reduces opioid requirements; particularly effective for constant background pain with allodynia (sensitisation); also treats neuropathic pain from diabetic neuropathy in FCPD
medicines.mechanism: Alpha-2-delta calcium channel subunit ligand — reduces excitatory neurotransmitter release (glutamate, substance P, CGRP) from sensitised dorsal horn neurons; reduces central sensitisation
medicines.side_effects: Dizziness; somnolence; weight gain; oedema; cognitive effects

medicines.name: Amitriptyline (Low-Dose Tricyclic Antidepressant)
medicines.dosage: 10-25 mg at bedtime; titrate to 50-75 mg maximum
medicines.use_case: Central pain modulation in chronic pancreatitis; improves sleep (often severely disrupted by pain); opioid-sparing; also treats neuropathic pain; start low and titrate slowly

medicines.name: Celecoxib — COX-2 NSAID
medicines.dosage: 200 mg once or twice daily
medicines.use_case: Adjunct for inflammatory flares in chronic pancreatitis; anti-inflammatory; less GI toxicity than non-selective NSAIDs; avoid in renal impairment

medicines.name: Opioids (Step 3 — Reserved for Severe Chronic Pain)
medicines.description: Strong opioids (morphine, oxycodone, buprenorphine) for severe chronic pancreatitis pain uncontrolled by steps 1-2 and failing interventional approaches; opioid dependence is a significant concern in chronic pancreatitis; use lowest effective dose; modified-release formulations preferred for around-the-clock pain; maximise non-opioid treatments first; involve pain specialist
medicines.india_note: Opioid accessibility for non-cancer chronic pain remains challenging in India due to regulatory restrictions; tramadol and buprenorphine patches are more accessible alternatives

medicines.name: Antioxidant Combination Therapy
medicines.description: Vitamin C 600 mg/day + Vitamin E 270 IU/day + Selenium 75 mcg/day + Beta-carotene 9 mg/day + Methionine 2 g/day — originally studied by Bhardwaj et al. for Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis at AIIMS Delhi
medicines.evidence: RCT by Bhardwaj et al. (Gastroenterology 2009): antioxidant combination significantly reduces painful episodes, hospitalisation, and disease progression in TCP; mechanism: corrects oxidative stress deficiency contributing to tropical pancreatitis aetiopathogenesis
medicines.india_use: Widely used in India for TCP management; standard inclusion in TCP treatment protocols at major Indian pancreatic centres (AIIMS, PGI Chandigarh, SGPGI Lucknow)

medicines.name: Octreotide (Somatostatin Analogue)
medicines.dosage: 100-200 mcg subcutaneously three times daily; LAR 20-30 mg IM monthly
medicines.use_case: Pancreatic fistula (duct disruption causing ascites or pleural effusion — octreotide reduces pancreatic secretion to allow fistula healing); refractory pseudocyst (reduces secretory pressure); octreotide test in chronic pancreatitis pain (reduces ductal pressure and pain in some patients); post-ERCP/pancreatic surgery prophylaxis

medicines.name: Steroid Therapy — Autoimmune Pancreatitis
medicines.dosage: Prednisolone 40 mg/day × 4 weeks; taper by 5 mg/week over 3-6 months; maintenance 5-10 mg/day if relapse risk high (IgG4-RD with multiple organ involvement)
medicines.use_case: ONLY FOR AUTOIMMUNE PANCREATITIS (AIP Type 1 and Type 2) — dramatic complete response expected; monitor response at 2-4 weeks with CT; complete resolution of 'sausage pancreas' and ductal changes; NOT for other forms of pancreatitis

categories.purpose: Manage pancreatogenic diabetes (Type 3c / FCPD) arising from loss of beta cell function in chronic pancreatitis.
diabetes_management_principles: Type 3c diabetes requires INSULIN in most cases — sulfonylureas are less effective (reduced beta cell mass); metformin can be used in mild FCPD but often insufficient
HIGH RISK OF HYPOGLYCAEMIA — absent glucagon counterregulation (alpha cell destruction) + malabsorption = unpredictable glycaemia; start with very LOW insulin doses and titrate carefully
MONITOR FREQUENTLY — due to erratic glucose variability from malabsorption; continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) is ideal where available
TREAT EPI FIRST — adequate PERT normalises nutritional absorption and stabilises glucose patterns before escalating insulin doses

medicines.name: Basal Insulin — Glargine / Degludec
medicines.dosage: Start VERY LOW: 0.1-0.2 units/kg/day subcutaneous at bedtime; titrate by 2 units every 3-5 days targeting fasting glucose 5-7 mmol/L; total daily insulin dose typically much lower than Type 1 diabetes (malabsorption reduces carbohydrate load)
medicines.use_case: Basal insulin replacement for Type 3c/FCPD; glargine (degludec has lowest hypoglycaemia risk — ideal for FCPD brittle diabetes)

medicines.name: Bolus / Prandial Insulin — Rapid-Acting Analogues
medicines.dosage: 4-6 units with main meals; reduce dose if poor oral intake; adjust based on pre- and post-meal glucose monitoring
medicines.use_case: Postprandial hyperglycaemia in Type 3c; bolus doses must be adjusted for actual food intake (malabsorption makes dose calculation difficult)

medicines.name: Metformin (for Mild Type 3c Without Severe Malnutrition)
medicines.dosage: 500-1000 mg twice daily with meals
medicines.use_case: Mild FCPD without severe weight loss; reduces hepatic glucose production; avoid in severe malnutrition, alcoholism, renal impairment

medicines.name: Insulin Infusion — Acute Treatment of Hypertriglyceridaemia
medicines.dosage: Insulin infusion 0.1-0.3 units/kg/hour IV; dextrose simultaneously if glucose <10 mmol/L; target rapid reduction of triglycerides (from >1000 to <500 mg/dL within 24-48 hours); insulin activates lipoprotein lipase dramatically reducing circulating triglycerides
medicines.use_case: Acute severe hypertriglyceridaemia-induced pancreatitis; insulin infusion is the most effective acute intervention to reduce triglycerides

medicines.name: Fibrates (Secondary Prevention)
medicines.dosage: Fenofibrate 145 mg once daily; Bezafibrate 400 mg once daily
medicines.use_case: Long-term prevention of recurrent hypertriglyceridaemia-induced pancreatitis; fibrates reduce triglycerides by 40-60% by activating LPL and reducing VLDL production

medicines.name: Omega-3 Fatty Acids
medicines.dosage: 2-4 g EPA+DHA daily
medicines.use_case: Reduce serum triglycerides by 25-50% (at high doses); adjunct to fibrates for severe hypertriglyceridaemia

diet_and_nutrition.overview: Nutritional management in pancreatitis is fundamentally different for acute and chronic disease, and requires individualisation based on disease stage, degree of exocrine/endocrine insufficiency, presence of malnutrition (particularly in TCP), and patient tolerance. The overarching principles have evolved dramatically: the old 'rest the pancreas — nothing by mouth for days to weeks' paradigm has been replaced by evidence-based early enteral nutrition; and the chronic pancreatitis dietary approach balances fat restriction (to reduce steatorrhoea) with adequate caloric density to address malnutrition.

early_phase_0_to_24_hours.approach: Initially nil by mouth (NBM) while severe vomiting, paralytic ileus, or haemodynamic instability is present; IV fluids (Ringer's Lactate) as primary treatment; antiemetics to control vomiting; NGO status should be as SHORT as possible
early_phase_0_to_24_hours.start_oral_feeding: Resume oral intake as soon as the patient can tolerate it — typically within 24-48 hours in mild pancreatitis; oral feeding is guided by clinical improvement (reduced pain, reduced vomiting, return of bowel sounds), NOT by enzyme levels (amylase and lipase do not need to normalise before refeeding)

refeeding_progression.low_fat_soft_diet: Start with low-fat, soft, easily digestible foods; no strict BRAT diet required — normal soft food is well tolerated; low fat content reduces pancreatic CCK stimulation
refeeding_progression.foods_to_start_with: Moong dal khichdi; plain rice with dal; yoghurt; boiled banana; clear soups; idli; plain toast; crackers; rice water (kanji); avoid fried, fatty, or spicy food initially
refeeding_progression.progression: Advance diet as tolerated over 24-48 hours; most mild pancreatitis patients tolerate normal low-fat solid diet within 48-72 hours of presentation; do not prolong liquid diet unnecessarily

fat_restriction_principles.overview: Low-fat diet is the cornerstone of chronic pancreatitis dietary management — reducing steatorrhoea symptoms and improving quality of life; however, severe fat restriction can paradoxically worsen caloric malnutrition (fat is the most calorically dense macronutrient); BALANCE: reduce fat while maintaining adequate calories
fat_restriction_principles.fat_target: 30-40 g of fat per day initially if steatorrhoea is severe; gradually liberalise with adequate PERT dose — the goal is to manage steatorrhoea with PERT, NOT by extreme fat restriction; with adequate PERT most patients can eat 40-60 g fat/day without significant steatorrhoea
fat_restriction_principles.medium_chain_triglycerides: MCT oil (coconut oil, MCT oil supplements) — absorbed without pancreatic lipase (directly absorbed by intestinal epithelium via portal vein) — VERY IMPORTANT in severe EPI; MCT provides fat calories without requiring pancreatic enzymes; can be used as cooking medium or supplement to increase caloric density

chronic_pancreatitis_nutrition.small_frequent_meals: 5-6 small meals per day (every 3-4 hours) — reduces the digestive load per meal; reduces postprandial pain (smaller meals require less pancreatic secretion against the stenosed duct); improves glycaemic control in FCPD (smaller, more frequent carbohydrate loads prevent large glucose spikes)
chronic_pancreatitis_nutrition.caloric_and_protein_target: Target 30-35 kcal/kg/day (higher than normal due to malabsorption losses); protein 1.2-1.5 g/kg/day (adequate protein for muscle mass preservation and mucosal healing); in severely malnourished TCP patients: 35-40 kcal/kg/day

items.food: Khichdi (rice + moong dal with minimal ghee)
items.benefit: Easy to digest; complete protein; low fat; high caloric density when prepared with MCT oil instead of ghee; traditional Indian post-illness food with excellent nutritional rationale

items.food: Idli, dosa (not fried — steamed or non-oily)
items.benefit: Fermented rice and lentil — probiotic; complete protein; low fat; easily digestible; good caloric density; frequent small portions
Highest quality protein (biological value 100); virtually fat-free; complete amino acid profile for tissue repair and pancreatic regeneration; affordable
High-quality protein; omega-3 fatty acids (anti-inflammatory — reduce pancreatic inflammation); low saturated fat; excellent for TCP malnutrition rehabilitation
Easy to digest; potassium; provides readily available calories without fat; good tolerance; natural antacid properties
Probiotics restore gut microbiome; easily digestible protein; calcium and Vitamin D (important in malabsorption from EPI); well-tolerated; probiotic bacteria produce their own lactase
Natural electrolyte replacement; potassium; easily absorbed; no fat; suitable during acute-on-chronic episodes

foods_to_avoid.reason: The single most important dietary intervention in alcoholic chronic pancreatitis; alcohol is directly toxic to acinar cells; even a single heavy drinking episode can trigger acute-on-chronic pancreatitis; alcohol withdrawal requires medical supervision; complete and permanent alcohol abstinence is the ONLY intervention proven to slow progression of alcoholic chronic pancreatitis
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: ZERO ALCOHOL — no 'safe amount'; not one drink; medical detox if physical dependence; naltrexone or acamprosate for alcohol dependence management; Alcoholics Anonymous and support groups

foods_to_avoid.reason: Stimulate CCK and pancreatic secretion; worsen steatorrhoea; trigger postprandial pain; specific high-fat Indian foods to avoid: dal makhani (cream and butter); poori/bhature (deep-fried bread); samosas, pakoras, bhajias (deep-fried); very oily curries; heavy cream-based dishes; ghee in large amounts
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: Strictly limit during active disease; with adequate PERT dose, most patients can tolerate moderate amounts of dietary fat; cook with minimal oil — steaming, baking, boiling preferred

foods_to_avoid.reason: Cyanogenic glycosides in inadequately processed cassava may contribute to tropical pancreatitis aetiopathogenesis; while the evidence is not definitive, TCP patients from communities where cassava is a staple should be counselled on proper cassava processing or switching to alternative carbohydrates
foods_to_avoid.india_relevance: Most important for Kerala, Tamil Nadu, and coastal Andhra Pradesh where tapioca (kappa in Malayalam) is a staple food; properly processed and boiled cassava has lower cyanogen content

foods_to_avoid.reason: Smoking is an independent risk factor for chronic pancreatitis (independent of alcohol); approximately 2× risk; acts synergistically with alcohol to accelerate progression; significantly increases pancreatic cancer risk in chronic pancreatitis; nicotine reduces pancreatic blood flow and impairs enzyme secretion regulation
foods_to_avoid.recommendation: Absolute smoking cessation; varenicline (Champix) first-line; NRT patches; bupropion second-line

foods_to_avoid.reason: Capsaicin stimulates gut motility and pancreatic secretion — may exacerbate pain in acute-on-chronic episodes; tolerated better in stable chronic disease

Rapid glucose spikes from simple sugars (sugary drinks, sweets, mithai) cause severe hyperglycaemia in absent-insulin-counterregulation Type 3c diabetes; particular care needed with traditional Indian sweets, glucose drinks, and sweet chai

sample_meal_plan_chronic_pancreatitis.principle: 5-6 small meals; low-fat; high-calorie; PERT with every meal; alcohol-free; smoke-free; adequate protein
sample_meal_plan_chronic_pancreatitis.early_morning_6_30_am: Warm water; amla juice (antioxidant); light exercise if able
sample_meal_plan_chronic_pancreatitis.breakfast_8_am: PERT capsule + steamed idli (2-3) with thin sambar (no coconut oil excess) OR moong dal chilla (2) + low-fat curd; weak ginger tea (no milk fat excess)
sample_meal_plan_chronic_pancreatitis.mid_morning_10_am: PERT capsule + banana or papaya; low-fat yogurt; rice crackers
sample_meal_plan_chronic_pancreatitis.lunch_12_30_pm: PERT capsule + small bowl rice + moong dal + steamed vegetable (lauki, carrot) cooked with minimal oil + egg white (1-2) or fish (steamed); plain curd
sample_meal_plan_chronic_pancreatitis.afternoon_3_pm: PERT capsule + plain toast or rusk + coconut water; light protein snack
sample_meal_plan_chronic_pancreatitis.dinner_6_30_pm: PERT capsule + khichdi (rice + moong dal, MCT oil ½ tsp) + boiled vegetable + small bowl of curd; avoid large meals; stop eating by 7-8 PM
sample_meal_plan_chronic_pancreatitis.supplements_daily: Vitamin D3 2000 IU; Vitamin E 400 IU; Vitamin C 500 mg; Selenium 75 mcg (antioxidant regimen for TCP); B12 (if deficiency); calcium citrate; PPI (omeprazole 20 mg to protect PERT enzymes)

alcohol_cessation.overview: The single most important and evidence-based lifestyle intervention for alcoholic pancreatitis — both acute and chronic. Complete and permanent alcohol abstinence: slows progression of chronic pancreatitis fibrosis (the only disease-modifying intervention); dramatically reduces acute-on-chronic pancreatitis episodes; reduces chronic pain frequency and severity; reduces pancreatic cancer risk; improves nutrition and quality of life. There is NO safe level of alcohol in chronic pancreatitis.
support_strategies: Pharmacotherapy: Naltrexone 50 mg/day (reduces alcohol craving and relapse); Acamprosate 666 mg three times daily (prevents relapse by GABA modulation); Disulfiram 250 mg/day (aversion therapy — causes severe nausea with alcohol consumption); Topiramate (off-label but effective)
Behavioural: Motivational Interviewing (evidence-based brief intervention); Alcoholics Anonymous (AA); Al-Anon (family support); Residential rehabilitation programmes for severe alcohol dependence

Medical detoxification: in-patient alcohol detox with benzodiazepines (chlordiazepoxide reducing protocol) for physically dependent patients — prevents withdrawal seizures and Wernicke's encephalopathy (Thiamine 200 mg IM daily before any IV glucose during detox)

smoking_cessation.reason: Smoking is an independent risk factor for both acute recurrent and chronic pancreatitis — independent of alcohol; the combination of smoking + alcohol increases chronic pancreatitis risk 5-fold vs neither habit; smoking independently increases pancreatic cancer risk by 2-3×; nicotine reduces pancreatic blood flow; impairs gene regulatory mechanisms in acinar cells
smoking_cessation.strategies: Varenicline (Champix) 0.5 mg once daily for 3 days → 0.5 mg twice daily for 4 days → 1 mg twice daily × 12 weeks (most effective pharmacotherapy — 3× quit rate vs placebo); NRT (patch + gum combination); cytisine (available India — plant-derived nicotinic receptor partial agonist; lower cost than varenicline)

nutritional_rehabilitation_tcp.overview: For Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis patients — most of whom are from low-income backgrounds with significant malnutrition — nutritional rehabilitation is as important as any pharmacological treatment.
strategies: Nutritional assessment: BMI, mid-arm circumference, serum albumin, pre-albumin, transferrin — baseline and monthly; Dietitian-guided high-calorie diet (35-40 kcal/kg/day); Daily PERT with all meals; Protein-rich foods: eggs, low-fat fish, moong dal; MCT oil supplements; Government food assistance programmes (ICDS, mid-day meal, PDS ration — nutritionist liaison to access entitlements)

Micronutrient correction: Iron (often deficient from poor diet and malabsorption), Zinc, Vitamin B12, Folate, Fat-soluble vitamins; Antioxidant regimen (Vitamin C + E + selenium + methionine + beta-carotene) — standard in Indian TCP practice (Bhardwaj regimen)

post_acute_pancreatitis_gallstone_manage.overview: After gallstone pancreatitis — the source must be eliminated to prevent recurrence (recurrence rate 25-30% within 6 weeks without definitive biliary management).
post_acute_pancreatitis_gallstone_manage.recommendation: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy: performed during same admission for mild gallstone pancreatitis (reduces recurrence and complications; safe when pancreatitis has clinically resolved); within 2 weeks for moderately severe pancreatitis; delayed until full clinical recovery for severe pancreatitis (8-12 weeks after resolution of local complications); ERCP for CBD stones at the time of initial presentation if cholangitis or persistent CBD obstruction is present

monitoring_for_pancreatic_cancer.overview: Chronic pancreatitis significantly increases pancreatic cancer risk — particularly hereditary pancreatitis (50-70× risk), TCP (5-10× risk), and alcoholic chronic pancreatitis (3-5× risk). New symptoms in a patient with established chronic pancreatitis (new or changed pain, jaundice, new weight loss, rising CA 19-9) mandate urgent investigation to exclude cancer.
surveillance: Hereditary pancreatitis (PRSS1 mutations): annual EUS from age 40 years (or 15 years after onset); CT alternating with EUS every 1-2 years; consider TP-IAT consultation
TCP/FCPD: EUS and CT every 1-2 years from age 40 or after 10+ years of TCP; baseline CA 19-9; any symptomatic change → urgent EUS/CT
Autoimmune pancreatitis (on steroids): beware steroid-masking of early pancreatic cancer — confirm complete response at 2-4 weeks; any residual mass warrants tissue biopsy

mild_ap.green_zone: Improving pain (NRS <5); tolerating oral fluids; HR <100; normal SpO2; urine output adequate; no fever; CRP stable or falling → advance diet; plan cholecystectomy before discharge; discharge when eating and mobilising
mild_ap.yellow_zone: Persistent pain >48 hours; rising CRP at 48h >150 mg/L; unable to tolerate oral intake → CT scan; HDU monitoring; consider enteral nutrition via NGT
mild_ap.red_zone: Fever >39°C developing after initial improvement; SpO2 <94%; rising creatinine; hypotension → possible infected necrosis; possible organ failure; ICU; CT scan urgently; FNA consideration

chronic_pancreatitis_outpatient.routine_review_every_3_months: Pain score; stool frequency and character (steatorrhoea assessment); FE-1 annually; HbA1c quarterly; weight and BMI; nutritional markers (albumin, pre-albumin); fat-soluble vitamins annually; CA 19-9 annually; alcohol and smoking status at every visit
chronic_pancreatitis_outpatient.alarm_features_urgent_assessment: New or changed pain character in CP patient; new jaundice; significant new weight loss (>5%); new onset of diabetes in CP patient; rising CA 19-9; new palpable mass → CT and EUS urgently to exclude pancreatic cancer

complications.description: Secondary bacterial infection of devitalised necrotic pancreatic tissue — the most dangerous complication of acute pancreatitis; occurs in 30-40% of necrotising pancreatitis; indicated by gas in necrotic collection on CT (pathognomonic); confirmed by FNA
complications.management: Step-up approach: meropenem IV → CT-guided drainage → endoscopic transluminal debridement → VARD → open necrosectomy

complications.description: Walled collection of pancreatic juice (no solid debris) forming from ductal disruption; affects 5-15% of acute pancreatitis and up to 30% of chronic pancreatitis; most resolve spontaneously (<6 cm, asymptomatic); treatment when symptomatic: EUS-guided endoscopic transmural drainage (first-line) or surgical drainage
complications.management: Watchful waiting if asymptomatic and small; EUS-guided transmural drainage (cystogastrostomy) for symptomatic, enlarging, or complicated pseudocysts

complications.description: Progressive destruction of exocrine acinar cells in chronic pancreatitis → fat, protein, and carbohydrate maldigestion → steatorrhoea, malnutrition, weight loss, fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies; occurs after >90% exocrine function is lost (late manifestation)
complications.management: PERT (Creon/Panzytrat) with every meal and snack; fat-soluble vitamin supplementation; high-calorie diet; MCT oil; dietitian support

complications.description: Endocrine insufficiency from islet cell destruction — affecting 20-60% of chronic pancreatitis patients; particularly severe in TCP (FCPD); brittle glycaemia due to absent alpha and beta cell function; high hypoglycaemia risk
complications.management: Insulin (carefully titrated low doses); PERT first; frequent glucose monitoring; CGM where possible; avoid sulfonylureas

complications.complication: Pancreatic Ductal Obstruction — Biliary and Duodenal Stricture
complications.description: Chronic pancreatic head inflammation causes fibrotic stricture of the intrapancreatic portion of the CBD (obstructive jaundice; biliary cirrhosis if chronic) and of the duodenum (duodenal stenosis, vomiting, weight loss); also: biliary stricture in AIP (IgG4-sclerosing cholangitis)
complications.management: Endoscopic biliary stenting (metal or plastic via ERCP); surgical biliary bypass (hepaticojejunostomy) for refractory strictures; lateral pancreaticojejunostomy (Puestow procedure) for combined ductal and biliary decompression

complications.description: Peripancreatic inflammation causing thrombosis of the splenic vein (most common) or portal vein; splenic vein thrombosis leads to left-sided (sinistral) portal hypertension with gastric varices (NOT oesophageal varices — distinguishing feature); gastric varices bleed without prior oesophageal variceal bleeding
complications.severity: Moderate to Severe (gastric variceal haemorrhage = life-threatening)
complications.management: Anticoagulation (if no contraindication) for acute portal vein thrombosis; splenectomy for symptomatic splenic vein thrombosis causing gastric varices; endoscopic treatment of gastric varices

complications.description: Leakage of enzyme-rich pancreatic juice from ductal disruption into peritoneal cavity (pancreatic ascites — very high amylase in ascitic fluid) or via transdiaphragmatic lymphatics into pleural space (usually left-sided pancreatic pleural effusion); DIAGNOSTIC: amylase >1000 IU/L in ascitic or pleural fluid
complications.management: Octreotide (reduces pancreatic secretion); NPO + TPN for 4-6 weeks; MRCP to identify ductal disruption site; endoscopic pancreatic duct stenting across disruption; surgery (Roux-en-Y pancreaticojejunostomy) for failed conservative management

complications.description: A pseudoaneurysm of the splenic, gastroduodenal, or hepatic artery from enzymatic digestion of vessel wall by leaked pancreatic enzymes; presents with sudden severe abdominal pain and haemorrhage (into pseudocyst causing rapid enlargement — 'sentinal bleed'; rupture into peritoneum; GI haemorrhage via pancreatic duct — haemosuccus pancreaticus)
complications.management: EMERGENCY angiography and transcatheter embolisation (treatment of choice — highly effective); surgical arterial ligation as fallback

complications.description: Significantly elevated risk in chronic pancreatitis of all types: hereditary pancreatitis (50-70× risk); TCP (5-10× risk); alcoholic chronic pancreatitis (3-5× risk); autoimmune pancreatitis (uncertain but managed with vigilance). The most feared long-term complication of chronic pancreatitis; detection is challenging because cancer-related symptoms overlap with chronic pancreatitis symptoms
complications.management: Annual surveillance (EUS alternating with CT) in high-risk chronic pancreatitis; urgent investigation of any new/changed symptoms; Whipple procedure (pancreaticoduodenectomy) for resectable head cancer; total/distal pancreatectomy for body/tail cancer; FOLFIRINOX or gemcitabine-nab paclitaxel for metastatic disease

complications.description: Severe acute pancreatitis triggers ARDS through: circulating phospholipase A2 cleaving surfactant phospholipids in the lung → surfactant destruction → alveolar collapse; inflammatory cytokines increase pulmonary vascular permeability → non-cardiogenic pulmonary oedema; pleural effusions restrict ventilation. ARDS complicates 15-20% of severe acute pancreatitis
complications.management: ICU; mechanical ventilation (lung-protective: low tidal volumes 6 mL/kg; PEEP; prone positioning for severe ARDS); treat underlying pancreatitis

key_points: TCP is the most important and distinctive form of chronic pancreatitis in India — occurring predominantly in South India (Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Andhra Pradesh) and affecting young non-alcoholic individuals aged 10-30 years

Pathognomonic imaging: large dense intraductal pancreatic calculi visible on plain X-ray (chain of calcifications across epigastrium); MRCP — extreme ductal dilation 5-15 mm with filling defects from stones

Fibrocalculous Pancreatic Diabetes (FCPD) — Type 3c diabetes in young individuals; extremely brittle and hypoglycaemia-prone; insulin always required; presents with ketoacidosis-resistant hyperglycaemia
SPINK1 N34S genetic testing available at tertiary Indian centres — screen all young TCP patients and first-degree relatives
ANTIOXIDANT REGIMEN (Bhardwaj protocol): Vitamin C + E + selenium + beta-carotene + methionine — the most evidence-based medical treatment for TCP pain in India (AIIMS RCT 2009)

Drainage procedures for large-duct TCP: ERCP with stone extraction; ESWL (extracorporeal shockwave lithotripsy) for large stones; lateral pancreaticojejunostomy (Puestow procedure) — excellent results for large-duct TCP with dilated duct; total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation (TP-IAT) for intractable pain in young patients (available at AIIMS Delhi, PGI Chandigarh)
FCPD nutritional management: severe malnutrition requires intensive dietary rehabilitation; MCT oil supplementation; PERT mandatory; government nutritional support programmes
Pancreatic cancer surveillance every 1-2 years (EUS + CT) from age 40 years or after 10 years of TCP

Acute pancreatitis in pregnancy occurs in approximately 1 in 1,000-10,000 pregnancies; most common in third trimester; gallstone pancreatitis is the predominant cause (30-50% of pregnant women develop biliary sludge; 10-12% develop gallstones)

Management: IV Ringer's Lactate (safe in pregnancy); adequate analgesia — opioids (morphine, pethidine) are safe in all trimesters; antiemetics (ondansetron — safe in 2nd/3rd trimester; limited data in 1st trimester); foetal monitoring

Imaging: Ultrasound first-line (no radiation); MRCP preferred over CT for biliary assessment (no radiation; safe in 2nd/3rd trimester); CT only if life-threatening emergency where benefits outweigh radiation risk
ERCP: can be performed safely in pregnancy with appropriate radiation shielding and minimising fluoroscopy time; indicated for severe cholangitis concurrent with pancreatitis

Cholecystectomy: best performed in the 2nd trimester (12-28 weeks) — safest window; avoid first trimester (organogenesis); avoid late third trimester (uterine size complicates laparoscopy); laparoscopic cholecystectomy is safe in 2nd trimester for severe recurrent gallstone pancreatitis

Hypertriglyceridaemia pancreatitis in pregnancy: treat with: dietary fat restriction (severely limit fat in diet); insulin infusion (safe in pregnancy; rapidly reduces triglycerides); omega-3 fatty acids (safe in pregnancy); fibrates are CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy
Gallstones are the predominant aetiology in elderly (declining alcohol use + increasing biliary disease with age)
Drug-induced acute pancreatitis more common in elderly due to polypharmacy
Greater comorbidities (cardiac, renal, pulmonary) increase mortality from severe acute pancreatitis; APACHE II score adjusts for age
IV fluid resuscitation requires careful monitoring in elderly (cardiac and renal reserve reduced — avoid over-resuscitation causing pulmonary oedema)

Malignancy must be excluded as a cause of acute pancreatitis in elderly without other explanation — ampullary tumour, pancreatic cancer causing ductal obstruction; MRCP and EUS for any elderly patient with 'idiopathic' pancreatitis

Autoimmune pancreatitis Type 1 predominantly affects men over 50 — always consider in unexplained chronic pancreatitis in elderly male with obstructive jaundice (do not miss — dramatic steroid response vs dangerous surgery)
PRSS1 gain-of-function mutations cause childhood onset recurrent acute pancreatitis progressing to chronic pancreatitis; autosomal dominant; high penetrance (80%)
SPINK1 N34S — most prevalent genetic risk variant for pancreatitis in India; heterozygous carriers in combination with other risk factors develop TCP or hereditary-like pancreatitis
Pancreatic cancer surveillance MANDATORY from age 40 (or 15 years after first episode): annual EUS is the most sensitive modality for early detection

Total pancreatectomy with islet autotransplantation (TP-IAT): removes the diseased, chronically painful pancreas; harvested islets injected into portal vein to engraft in liver — providing insulin independence in 40-70% of patients for years; prevents post-pancreatectomy diabetes; performed at AIIMS Delhi, SGPGI Lucknow for appropriate cases
Genetic counselling: autosomal dominant PRSS1 — 50% of children of affected individual will carry the mutation; discuss implications for family planning

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Viral pancreatitis (Coxsackie B, mumps, CMV, influenza) can trigger acute pancreatitis directly; influenza vaccination reduces viral precipitants of pancreatitis; patients with chronic pancreatitis are often nutritionally compromised with reduced immune competence — influenza can cause severe illness; reduces triggers for alcohol relapses (acute illness triggers drinking in dependent individuals)
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: All chronic pancreatitis patients; all patients with recurring acute pancreatitis; immunocompromised patients with pancreatitis

vaccinations_recommended.frequency: PPSV23 single dose; booster at 5 years for high-risk; PCV13 followed by PPSV23
vaccinations_recommended.reason: Patients with chronic pancreatitis frequently have malnutrition, exocrine insufficiency, and immunological vulnerability — increased susceptibility to invasive pneumococcal pneumonia and septicaemia; surgical pancreatitis patients (particularly splenectomy for splenic vein thrombosis) are functionally asplenic and at very high risk of overwhelming post-splenectomy infection (OPSI) — pneumococcal vaccination is MANDATORY before elective splenectomy
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: All chronic pancreatitis patients with significant comorbidity; all patients undergoing splenectomy (give 2 weeks before elective splenectomy or as soon as possible after emergency splenectomy)

vaccinations_recommended.reason: HAV and HBV can cause acute hepatitis which may trigger acute pancreatitis (hepatic pancreatitis — via bile duct obstruction or inflammatory cytokine release); patients with chronic pancreatitis who develop viral hepatitis have significantly higher complication rates; patients with alcoholic pancreatitis are also at risk for alcoholic liver disease — HAV or HBV superimposed on alcoholic liver disease is life-threatening; patients with chronic pancreatitis may receive blood products increasing HBV exposure risk
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: All patients with chronic pancreatitis; all patients with alcoholic pancreatitis; ensure hepatitis B vaccination in all unvaccinated adults with chronic pancreatitis or chronic liver disease

vaccinations_recommended.reason: Salmonella typhi chronic carrier state contributes to pancreatic and gallbladder disease in India; typhoid fever itself can cause acute pancreatitis through haematogenous spread to pancreas; in India: typhoid vaccination reduces overall enteric infection burden and its pancreatic complications
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: All residents of typhoid-endemic areas in India; particularly relevant for TCP patients from South India

vaccinations_recommended.reason: COVID-19 causes acute pancreatitis directly (ACE2 receptors on pancreatic ductal cells; inflammatory cytokine storm affecting acinar cells); COVID-19 infection triggers severe multi-organ failure disproportionately in patients with chronic pancreatitis and malnutrition; long COVID-19 may worsen pre-existing pancreatic insufficiency
vaccinations_recommended.recommendation: Follow national vaccination schedule; particularly important for chronic pancreatitis patients who are more susceptible to severe COVID-19 due to nutritional compromise

when_to_see_doctor: Severe sudden onset upper abdominal pain radiating to the back — URGENT hospital attendance; possible acute pancreatitis; do not wait
Any upper abdominal pain with vomiting lasting more than 2-4 hours — possible pancreatitis; serum lipase and urgent assessment needed
Known chronic pancreatitis with acute exacerbation (acute-on-chronic pain flare) more severe than usual baseline pain — hospital evaluation
New onset of fatty, floating, greasy stools with weight loss — possible exocrine pancreatic insufficiency; FE-1 testing and PERT initiation needed
New onset of diabetes (polyuria, polydipsia, weight loss) in a patient with known chronic pancreatitis or TCP — Type 3c pancreatogenic diabetes; requires insulin management and specialist review
Yellow discolouration of eyes or skin (jaundice) in a pancreatitis patient — possible biliary obstruction, CBD stone, or pancreatic cancer; urgent assessment
TCP patient with change in pain pattern — previously controlled pain becoming worse, or new back pain — possible pancreatic cancer; urgent EUS/CT
Young patient aged <35 years with two or more episodes of acute pancreatitis without clear cause — genetic testing (SPINK1, PRSS1); EUS for microlithiasis; specialist pancreatology referral
Rising CA 19-9 in a patient with chronic pancreatitis — possible pancreatic cancer developing; urgent EUS and CT required
Patient with alcoholic chronic pancreatitis continuing to drink — requires urgent addiction medicine referral alongside gastroenterology; alcohol cessation support
emergency_signs: Sudden severe 'worst ever' epigastric pain radiating to the back — possible acute severe pancreatitis — CALL EMERGENCY SERVICES (102/112); hospital admission, IV fluids, analgesia, CT evaluation needed urgently

Fever >39°C with rigors developing in a patient with known pancreatitis who was previously improving — INFECTED PANCREATIC NECROSIS or CHOLANGITIS — EMERGENCY; IV antibiotics, CT scan, possible ICU admission
SpO2 <94% or increasing breathlessness in a patient with acute pancreatitis — ARDS or pleural effusion — EMERGENCY oxygen and hospital admission
Confusion, altered consciousness, extreme agitation in pancreatitis patient — septic encephalopathy, hypoglycaemia (FCPD), or hypocalcaemia — EMERGENCY blood glucose check; call 102/112

Hypotension (systolic BP <90 mmHg) with tachycardia in pancreatitis — HAEMODYNAMIC SHOCK from fluid sequestration, haemorrhagic pancreatitis, or pseudoaneurysm rupture — CALL 102/112; IV resuscitation urgently
Grey Turner's sign (flank bruising) or Cullen's sign (periumbilical bruising) — HAEMORRHAGIC NECROTISING PANCREATITIS — extremely severe; EMERGENCY ICU admission
Sudden severe haematemesis or rectal bleeding in a patient with chronic pancreatitis — GASTRIC VARICEAL BLEED from splenic vein thrombosis OR pseudoaneurysm rupture into gut — CALL 102/112
Tetany (hands and feet cramping, Trousseau's sign positive, perioral numbness) in acute pancreatitis — SEVERE HYPOCALCAEMIA — IV calcium gluconate urgently; ECG monitoring for arrhythmia
Patient with FCPD found unresponsive or in severe hypoglycaemia (glucose <3 mmol/L, confusion) — HYPOGLYCAEMIC EMERGENCY — give 20 mL of 50% dextrose IV (or sugary drink if conscious); call 102/112

frequently_asked_questions.question: What exactly is pancreatitis and why is it so painful?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Pancreatitis is inflammation of the pancreas — a gland tucked behind the stomach in the retroperitoneum (the space behind the abdominal cavity). The pancreas produces powerful digestive enzymes (like trypsin and lipase) that are normally activated only in the small intestine. When these enzymes activate prematurely within the pancreas itself — due to gallstones blocking the exit, alcohol damage, or other triggers — they start digesting the pancreas's own tissue. This autodigestion causes intense local inflammation with massive tissue swelling, fluid release, and chemical injury to surrounding fat and organs. The pain is so severe because: the pancreas is a retroperitoneal organ (behind the peritoneum) — inflammation here stimulates very rich nerve networks supplying the upper back and flanks, causing the characteristic 'drilling through to the back' pain; the inflammatory chemicals (prostaglandins, bradykinin) directly sensitise pain receptors; the swollen pancreas pressing against the spine worsens the pain when lying flat. The characteristic relief from leaning forward (reducing tension on the inflamed retroperitoneal pancreas) is a useful bedside diagnostic sign.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis and why is it especially common in Kerala?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Tropical Chronic Pancreatitis (TCP) is a form of chronic pancreatitis unique to South and Southeast Asia — and India, particularly Kerala, has the world's highest prevalence. Unlike the typical Western chronic pancreatitis affecting middle-aged alcohol drinkers, TCP strikes young non-alcoholic individuals aged 10-30 years, most from rural low-income families. The pancreas develops massive stone formation within its ducts (large, hard calculi visible on plain X-ray — like a necklace of stones across the upper abdomen), extreme ductal dilation, and rapid destruction of both digestive and hormonal pancreatic function. Why Kerala? The disease is associated with a combination of: genetic susceptibility (SPINK1 N34S mutation — impairs the pancreas's natural protective mechanism against self-digestion); protein-calorie malnutrition in childhood and adolescence (reduces protective enzyme inhibitors); and possibly cassava (kappa/tapioca) consumption (cyanogenic compounds in inadequately processed cassava may damage pancreatic cells). Many TCP patients develop severe diabetes (FCPD — Fibrocalculous Pancreatic Diabetes) in their teens or twenties — a particularly dangerous form that causes unpredictable low and high blood sugars. Management requires PERT (enzyme replacement), insulin, antioxidant therapy, nutritional rehabilitation, and often endoscopic or surgical drainage procedures.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Can pancreatitis be caused by gallstones? How are they related?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — gallstones are the single most common cause of acute pancreatitis (40-50% of all cases). The connection: the common bile duct (carrying bile from the liver) and the pancreatic duct both open into the duodenum through a shared channel — the ampulla of Vater. When a gallstone (particularly small stones less than 5 mm that can slip out of the gallbladder) migrates and becomes impacted at the ampulla, it blocks both the bile duct and pancreatic duct simultaneously. This creates back-pressure in the pancreatic duct — causing premature activation of the pancreas's own digestive enzymes inside the gland, triggering pancreatitis. The pain from gallstone pancreatitis characteristically starts 30-60 minutes after a fatty meal (fat triggers gallbladder contraction, pushing stones into the duct). The definitive treatment for gallstone pancreatitis is: ERCP (endoscopic procedure to remove the CBD stone if it hasn't passed) AND laparoscopic cholecystectomy (keyhole gallbladder removal — performed during the same hospital admission for mild pancreatitis) to prevent recurrence. Without cholecystectomy, 25-30% of patients have a recurrent attack within 6 weeks.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Should pancreatitis patients receive antibiotics routinely?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: No — this is one of the most important and frequently misunderstood points in pancreatitis management. Antibiotics should NOT be given routinely or prophylactically for acute pancreatitis. Multiple large randomised controlled trials have conclusively demonstrated that prophylactic antibiotics in acute pancreatitis DO NOT reduce the rate of infected necrosis, organ failure, or mortality — and actually increase the risk of antibiotic-resistant organisms and fungal (Candida) infections. In India, antibiotic overuse in pancreatitis is unfortunately very common. Antibiotics ARE indicated ONLY for documented INFECTED NECROSIS — confirmed by: gas bubbles visible in the necrotic collection on CT scan (pathognomonic); positive culture from CT-guided needle aspiration; or clinical evidence of sepsis not responding to supportive care 5+ days into illness. When infected necrosis is confirmed, the antibiotic of choice is meropenem or imipenem — both penetrate necrotic pancreatic tissue effectively. Outside of infected necrosis, the mainstay of treatment is aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (Ringer's Lactate) — this is far more evidence-based and life-saving than antibiotics.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What is Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy (PERT) and do I need to take it with every meal?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: PERT (Pancreatic Enzyme Replacement Therapy) replaces the digestive enzymes that your damaged pancreas can no longer produce — specifically lipase (for fat digestion), amylase (for carbohydrates), and proteases (for protein). Without adequate pancreatic enzymes, fat and protein pass through the gut undigested, causing: greasy, floating, foul-smelling stools (steatorrhoea); severe malnutrition and weight loss; deficiencies of fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E, K). Yes — PERT must be taken with EVERY meal and snack (not before or after — during or at the very start of eating) to ensure the enzymes mix with food in the duodenum where digestion occurs. The dose is flexible — you or your doctor may need to adjust the number of capsules per meal to normalise your stools. TAKE WITH PLENTY OF WATER. ALWAYS combine PERT with a PPI (omeprazole 20 mg once daily) — gastric acid rapidly inactivates the enzyme capsules; the PPI reduces acid and protects them. Common formulations available in India include Creon and Panzytrat. Do NOT open the enteric-coated capsules and swallow the granules — the coating protects them from stomach acid.

frequently_asked_questions.question: Does drinking alcohol once in a while harm me if I have chronic pancreatitis?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: Yes — significantly. There is NO safe amount of alcohol if you have chronic pancreatitis, especially if alcohol was the cause. Any alcohol intake: directly poisons pancreatic acinar cells and triggers further inflammation; can precipitate an acute-on-chronic pancreatitis attack requiring hospitalisation; worsens pancreatic fibrosis and accelerates irreversible gland destruction; increases the risk of pancreatic cancer (already elevated in chronic pancreatitis). The widely discussed concept of 'moderate drinking' in health guidelines does NOT apply to chronic pancreatitis. Even people whose pancreatitis was caused by gallstones or other non-alcoholic causes should avoid alcohol — alcohol acts synergistically with other factors to damage the already-vulnerable inflamed pancreas. Complete and permanent alcohol abstinence is the ONLY lifestyle intervention proven to slow the progression of chronic pancreatitis. If you are physically dependent on alcohol (experiencing withdrawal tremors or sweating if you stop), please see a doctor before stopping abruptly — alcohol withdrawal can be dangerous and requires medical supervision.

frequently_asked_questions.question: What are pseudocysts and when do they need treatment?
frequently_asked_questions.answer: A pancreatic pseudocyst is a collection of pancreatic juice (the fluid produced by the pancreas, rich in digestive enzymes) enclosed in a fibrous wall — forming when a pancreatic duct is disrupted (by severe pancreatitis or chronic inflammation) and juice leaks into the surrounding tissue. Unlike a true cyst, a pseudocyst has no epithelial lining (hence 'pseudo'). On ultrasound or CT, pseudocysts appear as smooth, round, fluid-filled structures adjacent to the pancreas. The good news: the majority of pseudocysts (40-50%) resolve spontaneously over weeks without any intervention, particularly if they are small (less than 6 cm) and asymptomatic. A pseudocyst needs treatment when: it is causing pain or discomfort from pressure; it is enlarging; it has become infected (developing fever and sepsis); it is compressing the stomach, duodenum, or bile duct causing vomiting or jaundice; or it is bleeding into itself (acute expansion). The modern treatment of choice is endoscopic drainage — using an ultrasound endoscope to create a small opening between the pseudocyst and the stomach wall (EUS-guided cystogastrostomy), allowing it to drain internally without any external incisions or surgery.
